| Signed releases on branch `sec-release-signing` (2026-10-19) | Closes the gap that an administrator API key together with write access to the archive bucket could make every node run a binary of their own (the owner's list of 2026-10-19). **Design (8, 9.3).** Ed25519. The private key is the Worker secret `RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY` of the signer `pgcf-release-signer-dev` (`apps/release-signer`): Cloudflare secrets are write-only through the API and the dashboard (the signer's own code can read its binding, so Workers edit access to the account is access to the key), `release-signing.ts provision` makes the pair in memory and sets the secret through the Cloudflare API, and the key is in no GitHub secret, file or terminal (owner decision 2026-10-19: go for release signing, stored in Cloudflare secrets). The public key is `apps/node-agent/release-signing.pub`, which the agent's build reads as the constant `update::RELEASE_KEY` (a file that holds no key stops the build; the repository holds a public key of which nobody has the private half until `provision` replaces it) and which `register-node-image.ts` checks against. The signed text is `signedReleaseManifest`: the line `pgcf-release-manifest/v1`, the release id, the sha256 and size of the four binaries in a fixed order, the Debian snapshot, and the sha256 and size of the package lock (which pins every package and cloudflared). The image is not in it, and the kernel and package digest are derived from the lock. **Signer.** One route, `POST /sign`, no binding but the secret, a tracked `wrangler.jsonc` with no secret and no account id (five variables name the repository, its numeric id and its owner's, the ref and the workflow file). It authenticates the caller by the GitHub Actions OIDC token of its run (RS256 against GitHub's JWKS cached five minutes with one refetch per half minute for an unknown key id; `iss`; `aud` = its own origin; `exp`, `nbf`; `repository`, `repository_id`, `repository_owner`, `repository_owner_id` (GitHub's immutable ids, so that a freed and re-taken name does not pass), `ref` = `refs/heads/main`, `event_name` = `push`, `job_workflow_ref` = `ci.yml` at that ref, `runner_environment` = `github-hosted`), checks the body strictly as `ReleaseManifestFields` (the shared contract: no key beyond the facts), requires the release id to be `sha-<first 12 digits of the token's sha>`, builds the text itself with `signedReleaseManifest` and signs it with WebCrypto Ed25519. It keeps no state: Ed25519 is deterministic, so a second call with the same facts returns the same bytes and there is nothing to count; it does not limit what one token has signed (a valid token gets any digests signed as `sha-<its own commit>` until it expires), and one content per release id is the API's (409 for a different spec of a registered version, to whoever registers second), R2's (no overwrite) and the nodes' (every digest checked) work, with the owner registering the real build first. It logs the release id and a refusal code, never a token, key or digest. **Path.** The job `sign-release` (`needs: [check, node-image]`, a push to `main`, `id-token: write` and `contents: read` and no other permission, no secret, no environment, no cache restored, `pnpm install --ignore-scripts`; the credential for the identity token is in the environment of every step of the job, so the trust root is `ci.yml` on `main`, its pinned actions and the locked dependencies that `node-image` and `sign-release` run) downloads the release artifact by id, runs `sign-release.ts sign` (identity token for the audience `RELEASE_SIGNER_URL`, the manifest's facts to the signer, the answer to `release.sig`; it fails, never skips, when the variable is unset, the signer is unreachable or answers anything but 200 with a signature, or the checked-in public key is still the placeholder; a pull request signs nothing and its dry run says "not signed") and keeps `release.sig` as its own artifact; the registration script checks it with the checkout's key before it uploads a byte (`--release-key` names the old key for the release that rotates it); the API requires a 128-hex signature (400 without one), stores it in the immutable spec (another signature for a registered version is 409), shows it as `spec.signature` and serves it at `/node/v1/releases/<id>/release.sig`; migration `0077` removes the releases registered without one and their region assignments. The token and the account id come from variables whose names are on the command line, and the output is the fingerprint of the public key and the next steps. Rotation runs through a second signer (one Worker holds one write-only secret), so the old key signs the transition release and the repository variable moves afterwards. **Tests, written before the code.** Run red first (`ReleaseManifestFields` and the signer's modules did not exist; the provisioning and signing scripts' tests failed on the old commands). Contracts: `release-signing.test.ts` (7: the exact manifest text, what a signature covers and what it leaves out, ambiguous values refused, the registration's signature shape, the spec and the file name, the two classes, the strict fields of a signer). Signer, in workerd with a key and an RSA JWKS made at test time (35): the signature verifies over the text the agent builds, written out by hand, and is the same every time; a release of another commit, another name, any extra or missing or malformed field, a body over 8 KiB and a wrong content type are refused; 22 token rejections (audience, issuer, repository, owner, the repository's and the owner's numeric id, a missing id, an id as a number, ref, pull-request ref, event, dispatch, three workflow files, runner, commit), the time rules with the skew, 13 malformed or forged tokens (algorithm, key id, another key under the same id, another payload, unsecured), the key cache and the one refetch for an unknown key id, GitHub unreachable, redirecting or answering rubbish giving 503, a missing or malformed key or variable (the two ids included) giving 500, one route, and the logs holding the release id and no token, key or digest; mutation checks (no event, algorithm, audience or commit check) each turned a test red. Scripts: `release-signing.test.ts` (8, against a Cloudflare API on the loopback interface: the order, which shows the file still held the placeholder while the API was asked to set the secret; a refused secret leaves the file and echoes neither token nor key; an existing secret refused with and without `--rotate` after the one request that lists the secrets (no PUT, the file and the secrets as they were), a real key refused without `--rotate`, and the rotation to a Worker that holds none; an answer to the secret that never arrives; a missing Worker; a file that cannot be written; the variable names; the API base), `sign-release.test.ts` (5, against a stand-in token endpoint and signer: the audience and the bearer credentials, the exact facts, the file's mode; the placeholder asks nobody; the missing variables; a refusal, an unreachable signer and rubbish answers, none of which leaves a file or shows a token; no redirect and the address rules), `scripts/ci/release-signing-workflow.test.ts` (4: no secret, no environment, `needs: [check, node-image]`, no permission but the checkout's and the token's, no cache, `id-token: write` only on the signing job and the dispatch-only `external_probe` whose token the signer refuses, no step that could pass over the signing, and the signer's variables equal this workflow) and the registration script's test of a signature present, missing, malformed, another release's and another key's. API: `fleet-releases.test.ts`, `release-files.test.ts` and `openapi.test.ts` as before. Node agent, with the shared vector `releases` (every digest different): `update::tests` (8) and in `service::tests` an unsigned and a forged release refused with nothing downloaded and a signed one installed after them, and a maintenance order of a forged release failed with the class and no lock read. Migration `0084_single_archive_bucket.sql` drops `regions.backup_endpoint_url` as well as `backup_bucket`; the region API takes and shows neither (a body that names one is a 400). `ARCHIVE_BINDINGS`, `ARCHIVE_US` and `ARCHIVE_EU` were already gone from the code of this branch (no file outside this plan and the generated diagrams names them), and the private configuration drops the `ARCHIVE_US` binding and the variable. The runbook's per-region endpoint check and D1 correction, and the test of them, are deleted: no region row is read for the endpoint any more. **Red, then green:** the new test `names the one bucket's EU endpoint for a database in us-dev, which has no endpoint of its own` (a database and node in a `us-` region whose row held the general endpoint) failed first, the credential naming `https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` and not the EU host (1 failed, 10 passed in `archive-credentials.test.ts`); green once the credential took the variable and the column was gone. More tests: a missing, empty, `http` or account-less endpoint makes the credential `archive_credentials_unavailable`; the Tunnel is made in the account of the variable (another account's endpoint looks there and finds nothing) and an endpoint without an account answers the credentials read with 500 and writes no gateway; the fence is given the variable's account, and null for an endpoint that names none; the region API refuses both fields and the table has neither; the contracts refuse both on `Region` and `RegionCreate`; `0084` drops both columns, keeps every region with its children and lets a region be made without them. **Deploy order** (runbook step 1): the Worker with the variable first, `0084` second; the Worker of this change reads neither column, so it runs on the schema before `0084` (except `POST /v1/regions`), and the Worker before it cannot run after `0084`. (2) *The migration is `0084`* (main took `0083` for the credentials revision); the test, the runbook and every row follow. (3) *The rollback windows are exact.* The verification found that the runbook allowed a rollback until the revocation, while 11.1 sets the Worker's parent key to a token with no right on the old bucket and the rollback's first step redeployed only `ARCHIVE` and `ARCHIVE_BUCKET_NAME`: a rollback started between 11.1 and 11.4 would have had every credential for the old bucket signed by a key R2 refuses for it, every database would raise `database_archive_failing` and none could sleep, for up to seven days when 11.2 waits. The runbook now lists, step by step, what can and cannot be rolled back: step 1, the Worker until `0084` is applied and `0084` never; steps 2 to 4, what is in production depends on how step 2 gave the Worker its parent key (see the verification of 2026-10-23 below: a second token is in production from step 2 on and is retired like an earlier parent key; only the new bucket added to the token's policy leaves production untouched); steps 5 to 10, the whole rollback; 11.1 to 11.3, the whole rollback with its first step also putting `R2_PARENT_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `R2_PARENT_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` back to the token that named the old bucket and keeping the 11.1 token until X_NEW; 11.4 on, no rollback, fix forward; step 12, nothing to undo. Found while writing it: 11.4 deleted the token of the copy before 11.5 ran step 10's last pass, which needs it; 11.4 now keeps it and 11.5 deletes it after the pass. Both parent secrets are set in one `secret bulk` (two puts deploy twice and leave a mismatched pair between). The critic's item 10 order holds: new parent key, credential refresh, then a base backup, a WAL archive and a restore read on the new bucket, then the revocation. Tested in `single-archive-bucket-migration.test.ts`: the windows, the rollback's first step, the 11.x order and the copy token, each red by mutation of the runbook. **Private tool** `bucket_move.py` (not in Git): `copy` and `verify` take `--prefixes-file`, a round over the prefixes of the databases that are not deleted plus `node-images/` and `infrastructure/v1/`, reported as one round with `round_listing_started_at` and `next_since`; the checklist is rewritten under the runbook's step numbers (12 forward steps, the windows, rollback steps 1 to 7, the key retirement, migration `0084`, the endpoint variable); `selftest --repo` compares the trigger and the SQL of the checklist with the runbook's text and fails when the repository is missing (it skipped the comparison silently before). With this, the three blockers of the US1 preparation that are in code (the endpoint, the bucket mismatch, the migration number) are closed; US1 needs the deploy and the cutover. **Verification of that round (2026-10-23), fixed.** (1) *The cutover row contradicted the runbook and the tool.* It retired the old keys by revoking both earlier parent tokens, the token of the copy and every bucket-wide key together, which leaves no token for the last pass of step 11.5 (the pass that closes the old bucket's gap); it summarised the rollback without the parent key's restore for a rollback that starts between 11.1 and 11.4; and it described the tool as it was before the round (a checklist that named `0079` and knew nothing of `0082`, a copy with no prefix list, steps 1-20 and R1-R8, no key retirement, one `--prefix` a call, a selftest that compares through `ROOT`). It is rewritten from runbook 11.4 and 11.5 and the rollback's first step: 11.4 revokes the earlier parent tokens and keeps the token of the copy, 11.5 deletes it after the last pass, the rollback also puts the parent key back from 11.1 on, and the tool is described as it is. Step 1 now runs one read-only count before the deploy (live databases that do not name `<old>`; it must answer 0) and drops the `ARCHIVE_US` binding and `ARCHIVE_BINDINGS` from the private configuration. Tested: the new assertion in `single-archive-bucket-migration.test.ts` runs the runbook's SQL on the fully migrated schema (a live database naming another bucket answers 1, a deleted one is not counted); red by mutation (`<>` changed to `=` answered 5). The tool's checklist prints the same query and its `selftest --repo` fails against the runbook of the round before (`the bucket check of step 1 differs`). (3) *Step 8 named no compare and no delete command, and 11.5 named a tripwire that no step defined.* Step 8 now names `verify --from <old> --to <new> --since <next_since>` and `prune --from <old> --to <new> --before <T_B>` (dry run, then `--execute`); step 10 defines the tripwire as `inventory --from <old> --since <T_REWRITE>`. (4) The critic's item 34 asked W2-F to wait for the Workers VPC change. No branch with that change exists on 2026-10-23 and main does not carry it, so the wait does not apply; the overlap is small (`env.ts` and `wrangler.example.jsonc` lose the `ARCHIVE_US` binding and `ARCHIVE_BINDINGS`), so that change rebases onto this one. Only the API parses region rows, so the only deploy order that matters is the Worker first, then `0084` (step 1). Gates after the fixes (2026-10-23, main `c54fca03`, no Rust or infra file differs from main): the six generator checks of the contracts pass; contracts 25 files 298 tests (two new runbook tests of the second verification), API 108 files 1,093, Edge 119 in 3 files and 3 workerd tests, release signer 35, CLI 31, E2E scripts 90 (88 pass, 2 skipped), CI and operations scripts 118, node-image 71; typecheck of every project, eslint, prettier and plan privacy (0 findings) green. **Not run live:** all of it; the cutover waits for the owner's window. **Second verification of that round (2026-10-23), fixed.** (1) *The window of steps 2 to 4 was not exact.* The runbook, the cutover row and the tool's checklist said that neither the new bucket nor the new token was in use in production before step 5. That is false for the second option of step 2: a second token set as `R2_PARENT_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `R2_PARENT_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` is the Worker's parent key from that deploy on and the access key of every credential delivered afterwards (`crypto/r2-credentials.ts`). An operator who gave the move up before step 5, read that the token was not in use yet and deleted it with the empty bucket would have ended every credential issued since step 2: archiving fails (`database_archive_failing`) and no database can sleep until the rows renew. The runbook, this row, the cutover row and the checklist now say what is in production under each option. With the new bucket only added to the policy of the existing token, no secret changed and nothing signs for it; giving up takes it out of the policy only once the bucket is unused, and the old bucket stays in the policy. With a second token, that token is in production from step 2 on; giving up either keeps it as the parent key and retires the previous token, or puts the previous token back in one `secret bulk` and retires the second token, each retired as 11.2 retires an earlier parent key (after one credential lifetime, or after the forced refresh with the barrier, with the time its successor became the parent key in place of T_KEY) and never with the empty bucket. "If a step fails" no longer says that nothing in production changed before step 5, step 1's way back names the `ARCHIVE_US` binding and the `ARCHIVE_BINDINGS` variable that step 1 removed from the private configuration, and step 2 notes T_STEP2. (2) *The tool's printed sequence died on its second pass* (the private `bucket_move.py`, not in Git). `write_private` creates a file with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` and refuses to overwrite, but the checklist named one fixed file for repeated passes (`copied.txt` in step 8 and in every pass of step 10, `missing.txt` in step 10's tripwire, `missing.txt`, `extras.txt` and `copied.txt` in the rollback's steps 4 and 7). Reproduced against the tool's own fake S3: a second pass that copied a key did the copy, printed `failed=0` and died with `FileExistsError`, and the file still held the first pass's keys; `verify` wrote the extras file before the missing file, so on the rollback's second chained pass (the old bucket always has extras) the missing file was never written and the prefix check ran on a stale list, which could miss a named prefix's gap that no later chained pass reports again. Fixed in the runbook (a paragraph "The files of the cutover" before step 1) and in the tool: one directory made once for the whole cutover and deleted at the end (a file with a secret, the D1 export and the rewrite, as soon as it has served), file names per pass (`copied-<pass>.txt`, `missing-<pass>.txt`, `extras-<pass>.txt`, `clean-<pass>.txt`, `prefixes-<round>.txt`, with a repeated pass under a name of its own such as `10-1b`), and `copy` and `verify` now refuse an existing output file before they list or copy anything, and refuse an output flag that does not belong to the command (an ignored flag leaves no file, which reads as "the pass found nothing"; a round over `--prefixes-file` takes no `--copied-file`). Red first: the new selftest case died with `FileExistsError` after the copy; green once the refusal comes before any request (the fake S3's request log and its store are unchanged by a refused call, and a pass under a new name writes its own keys). Tested in `single-archive-bucket-migration.test.ts`: the window of steps 2 to 4 (red on the old sentence) and the per-pass file names of steps 8 and 10 and of the rollback's step 4 (red on the fixed names), and neither the runbook nor the plan repeats the false sentence. |
| G6 restore tool: chunked import, on branch `restore-chunked` (2026-10-20) | **Found live (2026-10-20).** The first complete infrastructure backup (day 2026-10-20, artifact `d1-control`, 31,785,799 plaintext bytes, 55 tables; the largest `usage_samples` 30,722 rows, `usage_hourly` 6,234, `lifecycle_events` 4,839, `operations` 3,518, `node_minutes` 1,817) decrypted, authenticated and held to its receipt, but its import into a fresh scratch D1 failed on all three tries: `wrangler d1 execute --remote --yes --json --file` exited 1 with the error body `{"D1_RESET_DO":true}` and no row read or written, the provider resetting the D1 Durable Object while it ran one 31 MB file. **What makes D1 reset (read against Cloudflare's D1 limits and debugging pages, 2026-10-20).** wrangler 4.145 sends `--remote --file` through the import API (init with the file's MD5, an upload to R2, ingest, polling), so the whole file is one provider operation. The documented size limits are 5 GB per imported file, 100,000 bytes per SQL statement, 2 MB per row and 10 GB per database, and 31 MB reaches none of them; whether the 30 s limit on a query or API request applies to an import is not documented. The debugging page lists four resets: a query "trying to write a large amount of information (e.g. GBs), and is taking too long", the isolate over its memory limit, CPU time over its limit (when "attempting a large import/export") and an internal error or code update (for which it says to retry), and advises splitting the work; the first is written for gigabytes, which 31 MB is not. `D1_RESET_DO` is not documented and the body names no reason, so **the cause among the first three is not established**. All three grow with the work one import does, and the file failed three times in a row, so the fix bounds that work and assumes no single number. **Fix.** `chunkSql` (replaces `schemaFirst`, reusing its statement scanner) cuts the decrypted SQL at statement boundaries into chunk files and `importArtifact` runs one `wrangler d1 execute --remote --yes --json --file` per chunk, in this order: the `CREATE TABLE` statements; the rows table by table, each table after the tables it references (the tool loads the `CREATE TABLE` statements into an in-memory SQLite and reads `PRAGMA foreign_key_list`, then Tarjan's components over the child-to-parent edges; a component of several tables, or a table that references itself, is loaded in one chunk whatever its size, the dump's `defer_foreign_keys` pragma opening every chunk); the rest (`sqlite_sequence` rows, indexes, triggers, views) as one chunk, a trigger's pieces kept together. Bounds `--chunk-bytes` 2 MiB and `--chunk-statements` 5,000, **starting values**: about a tenth to a fifteenth of the unit that reset, a few thousand of this database's rows, with a chunk's fixed cost (upload, ingest, poll) small beside them; a statement above the byte bound has a chunk of its own. After the last chunk the tool runs `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` and refuses a row, then counts tables as before. A failing chunk stops the run with `chunk N of M failed (S statements, B bytes): wrangler d1 execute failed (exit code C or timeout); D1 reset in its output: yes|no` (the yes or no is all the tool says of wrangler's text, which can quote SQL; yes means the token `D1_RESET_DO` or the word `reset` in it; the runbook halves the bounds on a yes, on a timeout and on a repeated no); the chunks before it are committed, there is no resume, and the existing refusal of a database with any schema object blocks a retry on it (the error says to delete it and create a new one). The chunks hold exactly the artifact's bytes (the pragma once per chunk more), checked before anything is imported; each chunk file is `0600` in the `0700` temporary directory and removed once imported; a chunk is stopped after 10 minutes and reported as `timeout`; nothing new is printed that can quote SQL (the chunk lines carry numbers). **Measured without the provider.** The migrations (80 files) create 54 tables (55 with `d1_migrations`), 57 explicit indexes, 27 triggers (four with an INSERT in the body, one with two body statements; none has a later body statement that begins with INSERT, so keeping a trigger's pieces together guards the classification by a piece's first words rather than answering something this schema does), one view and 68 foreign key entries, 13 of them pointing at a table created later (`regions` after `nodes`, `databases` and others) and none a cycle or a self-reference. wrangler's local D1 (`d1 migrations apply --local`, `d1 export --local`: 55 tables, 80,225 bytes) cut into 19 chunks of at most 6,000 bytes and 12 statements and run one by one with `d1 execute --local --file` exports the same sorted lines (80,225 bytes) and has an empty `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`. Chunking a synthetic dump shaped like the live one (a child table created before its parent, rows of 600 bytes) takes 0.28 s and 147 MB resident for 25.8 MB and 41,795 rows in its three large tables (15 chunks of at most 2,097,152 bytes and 3,670 statements) and 0.73 s and 187 MB for 77.5 MB (39 chunks; laptop, `/usr/bin/time -l`). **Tests** (`scripts/operations/restore-infrastructure-backup.test.ts`): the wrangler double now loads each file as one transaction with foreign keys enforced and, like the provider, resets a file above a size with exit code 1 and `{"D1_RESET_DO":true}`, fails the import call of a given number, and can run a database that does not enforce foreign keys. Red first: the reproduction (a 5,491,330-byte dump whose child tables come before their parents, a trigger whose body holds an INSERT, literals with semicolons, quotes and line breaks, against a double that resets above 3 MiB) failed on the unchanged tool with `wrangler d1 execute failed (exit code 1)`; the other new tests failed on the missing exports. Green: the reproduction imports in at least five chunks of at most 2 MiB and its objects, rows, sequences and `foreign_key_check` equal the dump loaded without foreign keys; the order, the chunk bounds with read buffers of 1 to 1,048,576 bytes producing the same chunks, a chunk boundary inside a literal that holds `;` and a line break, the cycle and self-reference rule with every way of naming a table, the chunk-3 failure (number, exit code, no SQL in the message, one wrangler call per chunk up to it, a second run refused with `database_not_empty`) and a foreign key left violated are each a test. Removing the parents-first order, the trigger rule, the cycle rule, the rest-as-one-chunk rule or the pragma at the head of a chunk turns at least one test red. Round 2 (independent verification) added: the double records the row statements of each file, and the reproduction asserts that no chunk holds more than 5,000 and one holds exactly 5,000 (its rows are about 230 bytes, so the byte bound is 9,000 rows away), a test on the dump of the splitting test with a byte bound of 1 MiB and three statements asserts the same for `chunkSql` (both go red when `current.length + count <= maxStatements` is removed from `fits`), and a test of the failure message (an SQL error at chunk 3 says `no`, a reset with the body on stdout or on stderr says `yes`, the sizes equal the file the double received, nothing of wrangler's text is printed), which failed on the round-1 tool with `chunk 3 of 6 failed: wrangler d1 execute failed (exit code 1); delete ...`. Round 3 (independent verification) found three defects, all fixed. (1) **A stopped wrangler was not reported as a timeout.** `execFile` stops a chunk at the timeout with SIGTERM, but `apps/api/node_modules/.bin/wrangler` is a pnpm shim for `bin/wrangler.js`, which answers SIGTERM by killing the real CLI and calling `process.exit(code ?? 0)`. Measured again against wrangler 4.145: `d1 execute <id> --remote --yes --json --file` against a local endpoint that never answers (`CLOUDFLARE_API_BASE_URL`) and stopped by `execFile` after 8 s gave `error` null, `child.killed` true, exit 0 and an empty stdout (the `--local` path exits 143); the tool then said `did not answer with JSON`, with no `timeout` and no yes or no. `wranglerRun` now tells a stop by `child.killed` before anything else, so exit 0, 143 or none all read `timeout`, followed by the yes or no. The test's double, like the launcher, exits 0 or 143 on SIGTERM and never answers the import; the chunk timeout is a new `chunkTimeoutMs` of `ImportDependencies` (default 10 minutes; the test uses 1.5 s). It failed on the round-2 tool with `did not answer with JSON`; testing `!error` alone for success, or telling the exit code before `killed`, turns it red. Stopping wrangler does not cancel the provider's ingest, so after a timeout chunk N may still be applied; the scratch database is deleted next, which makes that harmless, and the runbook gives `timeout` a branch of its own (halve both bounds once), because that a chunk running for 10 minutes has nothing to do with its size is not established. (2) **`no` did not prove that there was no reset.** The tool said yes only for `D1_RESET_DO`, the body of the live drill, while Cloudflare's debugging page words other resets "D1 DB exceeded its CPU time limit and was reset.", "D1 DB's isolate exceeded its memory limit and was reset." and "D1 DB storage operation exceeded timeout which caused object to be reset.", and wrangler 4.145 throws "D1 reset before execute completed!" when an import ends unfinished (`wrangler-dist/cli.js`). The yes now covers `D1_RESET_DO` and the word `reset` in stdout or stderr (`/D1_RESET_DO|\breset\b/`; still only yes or no is printed, now labelled `D1 reset in its output`); a text that holds the word for another reason costs one run with halved bounds, while a missed reset never gets them. The test prints each of the four wordings on stdout and on stderr and expects yes, and an authentication error and expects no; matching the token alone, stdout alone or always yes turns it red. The runbook says that `no` is only the absence of those words, and halves both bounds once on a repeated `no` at the same chunk before the report. (3) The header comment of the tool still advised running wrangler by hand on the decrypted file, which the runbook forbids (the whole file is what D1 reset); it now names the sizes, the exit code or `timeout`, the yes or no and the runbook. **Not verified:** the provider's own import of chunks (that it accepts a file that opens with the dump's pragma and takes chunks of 2 MiB and 5,000 statements), and the cause of the reset. **Live acceptance** is the operator running the drill (`docs/operations/infrastructure-backups.md`, steps 1 to 7) on the real artifact: after the receipt is saved, the object downloaded and a new scratch database created, `node scripts/operations/restore-infrastructure-backup.ts import --input d1-control.pgcfenc --keys-env PGCF_RESTORE_KEYS --receipt receipt.json --database pgcf-restore-drill --wrangler apps/api/node_modules/.bin/wrangler` must end with `foreign_key_check: no violations` and 55 tables, and the `d1_migrations` and `regions` counts of step 6 must match the live database. It is one wrangler run per chunk, about 18 chunks for the first artifact, a line per chunk, and a 10-minute stop per chunk. If a chunk fails, its line gives the sizes, the exit code or `timeout` and the yes or no, and the runbook says what each answer means |
| Keep-warm for the DatabaseActor measured on scratch Workers, branch `keepwarm-measure` (2026-10-19; D14 part a) | **Method.** Scratch Workers on the Dev account (`pgcf-kw-scratch-*`), deleted afterwards and checked by listing: 79 Workers scripts and 18 Durable Object namespaces before and after (after the Q1 repeat as well), none of the prefix left, the product Workers untouched. A caller Worker (colo AMS, where the laptop is routed; the objects answered from AMS) made the Edge's call: `idFromName`, hint `weur`, one RPC. A sample is one admission in a fresh object; the latency is the caller's clock around the call; the object reports its constructor and module ids (a new constructor with the same module is a hibernation resume, a new module a reloaded isolate). Variants were interleaved per iteration, one object of each probed in the same second; differences are medians of paired differences with 95 % bootstrap intervals; 48 samples per cell in Q1 and in the extension, 60 in Q2 and Q3; a p50 over an even number of samples is the upper of the two middle values (at most 3 ms above the median in Q2 and Q3, at most 12 ms in the Q1 repeat). **Q1, idle gap (real actor; one never-used object per sample, 48 per cell, 864 samples, 0 errors; p50 / p95 ms; share of probes that found a reloaded module).** The first Q1 reused one object for all seven gaps, so another sample touched it during the gap in 32–44 of 48 samples from 60 s on; it was discarded and the repeat gives each sample its own object (checked: 864 distinct objects, every prime found a new object), with gaps up to 1,800 s. Real actor: 3 s 51 / 556, 2 %; 8 s 47 / 335, 0 %; 15 s 54 / 560, 23 %; 30 s 194 / 553, 40 %; 60 s 211 / 577, 65 %; 120 s 268 / 551, 88 %; 300 s 250 / 609, 92 %; 600 s 316 / 635, 100 %; 1,800 s 352 / 637, 100 %. Minimal class: 36 / 371, 49 / 397, 45 / 329, 62 / 382, 61 / 442, 120 / 316, 155 / 428, 165 / 422 and 251 / 524 ms, with 0, 0, 25, 46, 58, 79, 96, 98 and 100 % reloaded. Up to 8 s the object stays in memory (191 of 192 probes found the same constructor); from 15 s every probe (48 of 48 in both classes at every gap) found a new constructor, a hibernation resume, which costs 41–51 ms at p50 up to 60 s while the module is still loaded (a warm object 36–49 ms). The step is the eviction of the module's isolate; it has no threshold, its share rises with the gap, and a probe that finds a reloaded module costs p50 263–352 ms for the real actor and 79–165 ms for the minimal class up to 600 s (251 ms at 1,800 s). The controls of the same run (the first probe of an object primed 2–44 minutes earlier, median 23) give the cold level: minimal 257 / 402 ms in the class of the Q1 jobs and 243 / 504 in a class that nothing else touched, real 300 / 557 and 412 / 761; 46–48 of 48 in each found a reloaded module. Busy minus quiet class, paired by iteration: minimal +6 ms (95 % −62..+46), real −40 ms (−126..+12), so activity in the class did not change the cold latency measurably. The real actor is at the cold level from 10 minutes (p50 316 ms at 600 s and 352 at 1,800 s against 300 and 412), the minimal class only at 30 minutes (251 against 257 and 243). The cold level differs between runs: the Q2 control below (first run) gave 256 / 447 ms real and 106 / 327 minimal, the repeat 300–412 real and 243–257 minimal, for a reason not found, so the size of a saving is known only within a run (every paired keep-warm comparison below favoured keep-warm). With no keep-warm, the first admission after 60 s of idle finds a reloaded module in most probes (58 % minimal, 65 % real) and costs p50 211 ms on the real actor. **Q2 and Q3, does a keep-warm work (real actor, p50 / p95 ms; probes at or above 100 ms; paired difference to the control with its 95 % interval).** None 256 / 447, 98 %. Alarm that re-arms itself every 4 s: 46 / 75, 5 % (−214 ms, −244..−138); every 8 s: 43 / 76, 3 %; every 30 s: 44 / 248, 20 %; every 60 s: 48 / 204, 28 % (−144, −216..−123). Cron trigger that visits every minute: 48 / 300, 33 % (−146, −200..−120). Visit loop every 5 s: 40 / 61, 3 %; every 10 s: 38 / 58, 3 % (−210, −264..−145). | Node observation reports no longer outrun the agent's timeout, on branch `observation-scale` (2026-10-19) | **Found live.** EU1 with about 235 databases posted observations that timed out for hours (`observation_not_posted`, class `http_timeout`, the agent's 20 s timeout), five creates stood `pending` for 30–60 minutes and the 300-database population stalled. **Cloudflare, not Contabo:** Workers Logs held 70 `POST /node/v1/observations` in an hour (the agent's attempts: every one arrived), the handlers ran 50–65 s (log lines of one invocation 64 s apart), the same node's desired-page reads answered in 0.3 s and a SQL through the Edge in 2.3 s, and the timeouts began before the firewall change of 11:18 UTC. **Cause:** `nodeObservations()` took the up to 200 databases of a report one after another, and each changed one waited up to 1 s for its own cold DatabaseActor's publish. **Fix:** the API takes eight at a time with a 12 s budget (a report with databases left unstarted is refused whole with the existing retryable 503, which both agent releases keep and re-post), the agent sends 64 per report with what is not asleep first and halves the batch after a timeout or 5xx, and a `node_observation_report` line logs every report that took 2 s or held 50 databases. Test first: 48 publishes of 200 ms took 10.2 s sequentially and 1.4 s with eight in flight. **Live after the API deploy (agent half still to release):** the first report held 200 observations and took 10.2 s (slowest 1.1 s, all accepted), the next 31 took 2.7 s, the backlog was gone within 13 s and the stuck creates completed. | Volumes out of PID 1's mount namespace (`MountImages=`) on branch `sandbox-v4h` (2026-10-19) | **What.** The agent unit has `PrivateMounts=yes`, so the volumes it mounts are in its own mount namespace. A database unit mounts its own volume (`MountImages=/run/pgcf/dev/<id>:/var/lib/pgcf/db/<id>:root:nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime`) from `/run/pgcf/dev/<id>`, a symlink that the agent keeps in a directory only root can use (0700, checked at every use) and that the unit asserts (`AssertPathExists=`): it is made by rename after the volume is attached, removed first of all before an unmount, a repair or a removal, removed when the pool's failure marks the volume suspect, and removed for every volume at the agent's start. Jobs mount the device of the generation they serve (a restore its target's). The image masks `modprobe@loop`, `@dm_mod` and `@dm_verity`, which `MountImages=` would run again for every start. **Why.** systemd's executor copies PID 1's mount namespace for every unit it starts and reads its mount table about 64 times (ftrace: 56 scans in the V4h unit against 3 for a plain unit), so the start of `pgcf-pg@` grew with the volumes mounted there, and PID 1 used 1,070 ms of CPU to mount 1,000 volumes where it used 0 ms when the agent's namespace does it. **Lab table** (median ms of 20 to 25 runs per cell after 2 warm-up rounds, rounds interleaved; N is the number of volumes present; the host has 21 base mounts; ext4 on loop devices unless marked; the unit's ExecStart is a static stand-in binary, not PostgreSQL). Executor handoff (exec of the executor to exec of ExecStart) at N = 17 / 164 / 300 / 1,000: volumes in PID 1's namespace 36.5 / 57.5 / 80.8 / 243.1 (p95 at 1,000: 496); volumes in the agent's namespace with the unit mounting its own 36.2 / 39.2 / 34.7 / 39.8; on device-mapper thin volumes (calm rerun) 34.8 / 63.6 / 89.3 / 272.5 against 35.8 / 35.4 / 40.1 / 35.5. `systemctl start` to ExecStart at the same counts: 50.4 / 65.9 / 88.8 / 234.5 against 52.8 / 55.0 / 52.0 / 53.8. A backup job's pattern (a tmpfs over `/var/lib/pgcf` and a bind of the volume) 54.7 / 114.6 / 259.0 / 2,150.7, which grows faster than linearly (about with the square of N), against 54.0 at 164 and 55.5 at 1,000 with `MountImages=`. Running units do not slow a start: 55.3 / 53.3 / 51.1 / 56.0 at 0 / 164 / 300 / 900 awake units (1,000 volumes), against 286.9 (none awake) and 261.7 (300 awake) with the volumes in PID 1's namespace. **Caveats.** One Debian 13 container with systemd 257.13 as PID 1 in a laptop VM (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, 6 vCPU, Apple silicon), shared with other workloads (every cell has a plain unit as a noise control); not EU1's kernel (6.12) or hardware; small volumes; the start path only, no data-plane or I/O effect measured. **The 6.6 times is unverified.** EU1's executor handoff before the change was 105 ms at 17 and 245 ms at 164 volumes, about 1 ms per volume, which is 6.6 times the lab's slope between those two counts (0.14 ms per volume) and 4 to 5 times its four-point slope; the cause of the factor is not found (kernel, hardware, the node's other mounts and the lab's devices are candidates), so only the shapes transfer (linear in N with the volumes in PID 1's namespace, flat with them in the agent's) and the milliseconds do not. The effect on EU1 is not measured (11.2). **The device policy is wider.** `MountImages=` adds `block-device-mapper`, `block-blkext` and `block-loop` (`rwm`) and `/dev/mapper/control` and `/dev/loop-control` (`rw`) to the unit's `DeviceAllow`, next to the `char-rtc r` it had; `systemctl show -p DeviceAllow` lists exactly these six, the units' lab and the boot test assert it, and it cannot be avoided while `MountImages=` is used. What neutralises it, checked as the unit's user in the lab: the unit's private `/dev` has no block node, `mknod` fails, and a device-mapper node by its number and the volume's device by its name cannot be opened (the probe fails with 35 block nodes when `PrivateDevices=` is turned off); behind that stand the empty capability set, `NoNewPrivileges=yes` and the nodes being `root:disk 0660`. **What stays visible.** The ids and generations of every database (`/etc/passwd`, `/run/pgcf`, `/sys/block/dm-*/dm/name`), a neighbour's I/O and write counters (`/sys/block/dm-*/stat`, `/sys/fs/ext4/dm-*`) and its `memory.current` and `cgroup.procs` (`/sys/fs/cgroup/pgcf.slice/pgcf-pg@<id>.service`) stay readable through sysfs and the cgroup tree, as before; the isolation keeps data and volumes out of reach and does not hide other databases. **A volume made before the gap.** Every filesystem is now made and grown 4 MiB (one extent) before the end of its volume, because image dissection refuses a device that carries a RAID or ZFS signature where libblkid probes, and the farthest probe (`promise_raid`) reads 3,087 sectors (1,580,544 bytes) from the end (lab, libblkid 2.41.5: a Promise signature there made `blkid -p` call an ext4 device a RAID member, and one sector farther from the end it did not), so tenant data can never form one there. The risk accepted for Dev: a volume made before the gap, which is every volume on EU1 today, fills its volume and has no such protection until it grows, so a tenant that knew the prober could make it refuse its mount and its database could neither start nor archive. The migration is to recreate the databases, or to shrink the filesystem offline while the database sleeps (`e2fsck -f`, then `resize2fs <device> <volume size - 4 MiB>K`); the reinstall that brings the image to a node (11.2) makes every volume again, with the gap. A grow to the size a filesystem already has is skipped, because `resize2fs` refuses to shrink one for ever (lab: "On-line shrinking not supported"). |
| Volume sandbox: review fixes and the rule for a held volume, on branch `sandbox-v4h` (2026-10-19) | An independent review of the commit above found 11 things, and a second review of the fixes found a data-safety gap, a test double that did not follow the node, and rows that did not reach the plan; each was checked in the code, and each real one was fixed with its failing test first. **The agent's mount table is no witness.** The agent's namespace ends with the agent, and a unit or a job mounts a volume in a namespace of its own, so a test double that reported every volume mounted for ever hid the places that read it. The double now follows the node: its mounts and links end with an agent restart, a unit keeps the volume it started on, a start without the link fails its assertion, and an unmount, a removal (lvm2: "in use") and a repair are `Busy` while a running unit or a job holds the volume (`hold_volume` and `release_volume` stand for a job with `MountImages=`), and the next generation is neither made nor mounted then (`OtherGeneration`). (1) A restarted agent with no record of a database stops the unit of a superseded generation by the unit's own `/proc/<pid>/mountinfo` (`Machine::unit_volume`); an answer that cannot be read leaves the order `unit_not_stopped`. (2) The pool's failure tags every volume whose device is open (`lv_attr` `o`), and ext4's errors are read from `/sys/fs/ext4/dm-<minor>`, wherever the filesystem is mounted. (3) The detach looks for ext4's entry after the agent's own unmount (waits 250 ms; the entry went 1 to 2 ms after a holder ended, 20 runs), mounts the volume again and answers `Busy` if it stays; `debugfs -w` writes a filesystem that another namespace has mounted where `e2fsck` stops with 8 (lab), so no repair starts on a held volume. (4) The 4 MiB gap (above). (5) `resize2fs` is skipped for a filesystem that has the size. (6) The lock split of `mount_all` and its fairness test are deleted (no observed problem). Lab, 300 volumes of 32 MiB, serial under the storage lock: `mount_all` of 50 / 100 / 300 volumes took 0.20 / 0.26 / 0.86 s at first and 0.17 / 0.30 / 0.89 s after the rule below (about 3 ms each), and unmounting 300 took 1.1 s. (7) The rollout order is in 11.2. (8) A wake and a recovery ask whether the volume is attached (the link), not whether its directory is a mount. (9) `pgcf-agent check` refuses to run in PID 1's namespace. (10) The unit's user finds no block node in `/dev` and cannot make or open one (lab and boot test). (11) The job-device test is a plain test. **The rule for a held volume (data safety, found by the second review).** After an agent restart the boot's `mount_all` mounts only the generation the page names, and the detach, the `create_volume` check, the repair and the removal each looked at the agent's own mount table, so a unit that still ran on the old generation was invisible: the next generation could be built, mounted and linked, and a later start of `pgcf-pg@<id>` would have been a no-op on the old unit (systemd leaves a running unit as it is), so the database would have gone on running on the old volume while the agent believed it ran on the new one. Reproduced in the storage lab on the old logic: `unmount_volume` and `create_volume` answered Ok and the new volume was built, mounted and linked while a unit held the old one. The rule, stated in Appendix C and the node-image README: a volume is detached, and a generation of a database is made or mounted, only while no filesystem of that volume (for a detach) or of another generation of the same database (for a make or a mount) is alive in any mount namespace, which ext4's `/sys/fs/ext4/dm-<minor>` entry says (it exists while a superblock does), with or without a mount of the agent's own. A held volume answers `Busy`, a held other generation `OtherGeneration`, and lvm2's own refusal of an open device is the removal's `Busy`. `attach` is the one place that mounts a generation (create, boot, wake, recovery, grow), so the check is there, and in `create_volume` before anything is made. The build releases the previous generation before it writes anything, and ends `build_failed` when it cannot, leaving the record of the old generation as it was, so the next pull releases it again; before, the build went on, wrote the new generation's record, and the retry never released the old volume again (red in the agent test with the faithful double). The plan step does not forbid a build while a unit runs, because a build that a crash stopped resumes with its own recovery unit running on the new generation; the kernel rule needs no such exception. **Tests.** Failing first: three unit tests of the rule on a recorded `lvs` (detach, create, attach); the storage lab test of the restart with the old generation held only by a unit (red on the old logic because the boot mounted the next generation; now `mount_all`, `mount_volume` and `create_volume` refuse, `unmount_volume`, `recover_volume` and `remove_volume` answer `Busy`, the unit's own view of its data is unchanged, and everything goes through once the unit has stopped); the node lab on real systemd and LVM (red on the old logic with `Ok(())` for the unmount); an agent test in which a move target is not built while the unit of the source runs after a restart and is built once it has stopped (red on the old logic: the record was overwritten and the retry never released the volume). The Busy paths of the agent run against the faithful double: a release followed by a build, a recovery that tries again until a job lets go, and a superseded order that ends `volume_not_removed` and is followed by one that removes the volume. `testpg::bin_directory` now fails when there is no PostgreSQL 18 and `CI` is set, instead of letting the tests that need one skip: the Rust step of CI runs `cargo test --workspace` with the pinned PostgreSQL 18.6, which is where the agent's tests, the new ones included, run (red against the old behaviour in a unit test of the guard); the job-device test needs no database. Gates: the contracts checks, typecheck, eslint, prettier, plan privacy, the image's units tests (14), fmt, clippy with and without the lab cfg, 518 lib tests (511 at the merged HEAD, 13 ignored) in the pinned builder image with PostgreSQL 18.6, contrib (`pg_prewarm`) and `ps` as a non-root user, the storage lab (28 tests), the systemd lab (12: units 10, node 1, job 1) and Mermaider. The storage lab's full-pool test depends on writeback timing: under CPU load it failed 3 of 6 runs both at the commit before and after the first round, and passed in every quiet run. |

Kept rows (24 to 25 hours): about 50,000 and about 372,000. **D1 rows written:** the insert of one sample wrote 5 rows in the test D1 (the row, three indexes, the revision row the trigger upserts); the prune is bounded at the same 5, so 10 over a sample's life. 300 and 5 %: 7.3 million a month for inserts, 14.7 million with the prune (before 4.3 and 8.6): +6.0 million, 6 USD at 1 USD per million beyond the 50 million included a month. 1,000 and 20 %: 54.7 million and 109.4 million (before 14.4 and 28.8): +80.6 million, 81 USD (40 USD for the inserts alone); the included 50 million is shared with every other write of the account, so the increase is the marginal figure. Reads stay far inside the included 25 billion (about 1 billion a month for 200 awake databases, an estimate from the per-request hour count). Metrics only; the price is the integrator's. **Alert IDs.** `event_id` is now a function of the error: a version 8 UUID (RFC 9562; the first version said 5, but a name-based UUID from SHA-256 is no version 5, which is SHA-1, so an integrator with a UUIDv5 library would not have reproduced it) from the SHA-256 of a fixed domain string, the region, the kind and the sorted subjects the event lists (`alertEventId`; a kind without subjects, region and kind alone), instead of a random UUID per episode. `control_cron_step_failing` lists no database or node, so a failing cron step is its subject: the steps with 5 or more consecutive failures (`identity` of the observation, passed only to `alertEventId`; a step that failed once is not part of the error, and an active episode whose failing step changes keeps its event, as before), so `usage` failing one day and `health_alerts` the next have two IDs, and `usage` failing again has the first one again. The backup kinds list `d1` only (`infrastructureBackupHealth` expects one artifact kind), so region and kind are their whole identity there; `etcd` stays in the contract for old payloads. The same error keeps its ID through a clear and a recurrence; a different set of subjects is a new error with a new ID and is announced as before (only the ID generation changed: a subject that joins replaces the event, one that leaves changes nothing). The row (region, kind) reopens with the same ID (the `ON CONFLICT(region_id, kind)` takes precedence over the `UNIQUE(event_id)` that the same row also meets), `delivered_at` and `last_attempt_at` reset for the new episode, and the open episode is not sent again. `occurred_at` is the episode start, so a recurrence differs from the first episode in the payload. The listed subjects (at most 64) are hashed, because the payload and the re-announcement rule use that list and the full failing set is not read; a list cut at 64 changes ID when its head changes and returns to an earlier ID when the set returns; `unresolved` subjects are neither listed nor hashed. Consequences handled: the `Idempotency-Key` is `<event_id>:<occurred_at>` (Resend refuses a different body under a key it knows for 24 hours, so a recurrence under the bare `event_id` could not be mailed; not run against Resend), and the claim, the clearing and the replacement of an episode now compare the stored payload as well as the ID, because the ID no longer tells two episodes apart. Receivers deduplicate the pair `event_id` and `occurred_at`; a known `event_id` with a new `occurred_at` is a recurrence. The cron kinds are raised in every region and the region is part of the hash (`UNIQUE(event_id)` allows no ID in two rows), so one cron stall is announced as one event per region with a different ID each; one ID across regions would need a schema change and is not done. The `Idempotency-Key` code strict-parses the stored payload, like `infrastructureAlertStatus` does; a payload that does not parse is logged as `transport` and retried. **Deviation from the owner's request (owner decision).** Samples every minute are taken for databases that are not hibernated only; a hibernated database stays at one per quarter hour, so `health.disk` of a sleeping database reads `unknown` (no sample within 180 s) for 12 of every 15 minutes and `storage` is up to 15 minutes old. Sampling sleeping databases every minute too would add 285 x 1,344 x 30 = 11.5 million samples a month at 300 databases and 5 % awake (about 115 million D1 rows written with the prune, about 115 USD) and 800 x 1,344 x 30 = 32.3 million samples at 1,000 databases and 20 % awake (about 323 million rows, about 323 USD). **Review.** An independent review found six things, all checked against the code and all real: the hibernated mark (fixed failing-test-first), the version label (known answers recomputed with `node:crypto`), the shared ID of different cron steps (fixed failing-test-first; its backup half is not reachable, see above), and three texts (the stale OpenAPI sentence, the 15-minute wording of `health.disk`, and the replacement rule, which now names the exception that the three per-node warnings replace their episode only when none of the listed nodes still exceeds), and the receiver note (under Open). **Open (not done).** (a) Before the deploy: check or update the configured receiver so that it deduplicates the pair `event_id` and `occurred_at` (or the `Idempotency-Key`); a receiver on the old rule (deduplicate `event_id`) would acknowledge and then discard every recurrence (the receiver acknowledged four episodes on 2026-10-19 under the old contract). (b) Live acceptance after the deploy: one recurrence delivered through the real receiver with the same `event_id` and a new key; `storage` and `health.disk` of an awake database following a live fill minute by minute; and, separately, the 80 % and 90 % alerts for slow growth (the fill that passes both bands inside one report interval raises only the 90 % alert, the report cadence, not a defect). **Proof.** Red on the old tree: `node-intake.test.ts` 2 of 16 failed (per-minute and hibernated cadence; the newer sample behind `health.disk` and the rollup), `database-alerts.test.ts` 4 of 13, `infrastructure-alerts.test.ts` 3 of 12, `cron-watchdog.test.ts` 1 of 5, `infrastructure-backups.test.ts` 1 of 20, `alert-event-id.test.ts` (known-answer vectors) failed. Red on the first version of the branch, before the review fixes: the hibernated database that reports only in minutes 1 and 2 of a quarter hour got no sample (and a report at minute 7 of a quarter hour, none until minute 15), the test for a version 8 UUID failed, and two different failing cron steps got one `event_id`. Green after: all of them, the API suite (105 files, 987 tests) and the contracts tests (19 files, 224 tests); the known-answer IDs were recomputed independently with `node:crypto`, and `InfraAlert.shape.event_id` accepts version 8. | A request is not fenced when the page with the claim of its wake reaches the table, on branch `gateway-fenced` (2026-10-20) | **Found live** (EU1, agent and gateway of main `1ace7446`, the 5.3 cold gate sampler, Worker arm `http-batch` through the public hostname): 14 of 59 cold first requests (one HTTP `/sql` transaction of 6 statements, databases asleep for over an hour) failed, and 45 of 59 failed or took 1 s or more (p50 1,266 ms, p95 2,265 ms). In all 14 the agent had started the database (`wake outcome=started`, 293–419 ms) and the Edge had admitted the request, but the gateway logged `sql_stages` with outcome `fenced`, `dial_ms` 0, `auth_ms` 68–467 and `query_ms` 0: the request had logged in to PostgreSQL and was refused at its first statement, and the client got 400 with 57P03. The same requests against the then-warm database took 275–339 ms. **Cause.** A request took its admission epoch from the table when the wake was released, and `write_admitted` refused every write once the epoch of the database had moved. That epoch moved on any change of the database's entry. The agent publishes the entry twice for every wake: at the release (the claimed generation and operation, the entry's route revision) and again when the page that carries Cloudflare's claim arrives. The DatabaseActor commits that claim in D1 beside the request and hints the node, which pulls the page, so the second publication can land between the release and the first statement of a request, whose login took 68–467 ms in the failures (request 363–775 ms in all). It changes the route revision and nothing else (`Core::accept` and `table_entry`; the agent test below pins it), yet it moved the epoch. The WebSocket paths had the same fault: `actions.changed()` fires for every signal including `Running` (in the startup of `serve_socket` and of `serve_held`, and in the password login of `run_session`), and `dialable` and `admitted_at` compared the epoch, so a warm or cold connection that was starting up in that window ended with 08006. A second, narrower window: `admit` read the table again after `wake_state` had released the ticket and demanded the route revision equal, so a claim between the two reads answered `route_stale`. The independent verification found that the first fix closed it for the HTTP path and for a held wake only: a v5 ticket the table had released at once on the WebSocket path, which is the path a second connection takes right after a wake, when the claim's page arrives, was still admitted with no released unit and so under the exact revision (`serve_socket`). A table writer queued behind a long `write_admitted` or `write_running` read lock lands between the two reads, because tokio's lock is fair. **Fix.** The epochs are gone (`LocalTable::bound_epoch`, `database_epochs`, the table epoch, `Epoch`, `Backend::epoch`, `admitted_at`). What a session was admitted on is the unit, and the table says it still stands: `write_admitted` and `dialable` ask only that the database admits new work (`admits`: table current, mode running) and that the writer is the session's (`permits`: socket, uid, PID and invocation ID). A quiescing, sleeping or retired database, a table that is not current and a replaced unit are refused with nothing written, as before; a later route revision or the same entry again no longer fences (and, by construction and without a test, a quiesce that was resumed before the write does not either). A pooled HTTP session is reused on the same writer and at the generation it was admitted at (`Backend::generation`, checked against the route's in `checkout`), and the route revision does not matter: the claim's page moves only the revision, so the fix above holds, but a role change does not: `resetPassword` moves the database generation (`apps/api/src/domain/roles.ts`), the agent publishes the new generation on the same writer (`Core::accept`, then `set`), and `roles::apply` writes the new verifier without ending the sessions of the role, so a session of the old generation proved a password that PostgreSQL may no longer accept and would be served from the pool for up to `LIFETIME` (60 s) with PostgreSQL never asked again. A session of another generation is ended at checkout and the request logs in itself, so a reset password is refused (28P01) as soon as the node applies it, as before this change (the epoch used to refuse the reuse by moving on every entry change); found by the independent verification, which reproduced it. A session that is starting up is interrupted by an action other than `Running` (`sessions::until`, which `retired` of HTTP SQL shares). A released wake is admitted under the route revision of its release or a later one, as `wake_state` releases it; a route the Edge signed still names the revision exactly. A ticket is admitted through `Gateway::admit_wake(ticket, unit, revision)`, which builds the route of the released wake and admits it with a later revision allowed; the HTTP request (`wake`, at both of its releases: at once and after the hold), the connection routed at once (`serve_socket`) and the held connection (`serve_held`) call it, and `Gateway::admit` demands the revision exactly (the `released` argument and `admitted_wake` are gone). That is a convention and not a type: `admit` takes any `Route`, the fields of `Route` are public, and `Route::released` is a public constructor of the protocol crate that `serve_held` also uses for its startup check, with no unit, so nothing in the types stops a path from admitting its ticket exactly, and the race tests below, one per path, are what pin each of them. A type that would enforce it is a second route type in the protocol crate; no path has been seen to need one, and it was not built. **Tests, failing first.** HTTP (`tests/sql.rs`, the PostgreSQL double now waits at a gate before it answers a StartupMessage, so the order is fixed by the test and not by a delay): a cold request is released, logs in, the claim's entry is published under a later revision, and the login goes on; it failed with the live signature (`sql_stages` outcome `fenced`, 400/57P03) and answers 200 now. WebSocket (`tests/transport.rs`): a warm connection admitted before its StartupMessage, a held wake that is released while its pipelined password is incomplete, and a held wake whose pipelined password the gateway proves to PostgreSQL itself (the Neon driver's default; the double holds the login at its gate after the StartupMessage, the claim's entry and the channel's `Running` are published, then the gate opens, and the client gets AuthenticationOk), each followed by the entry under a later revision and the channel's `Running`; all three ended `fenced` (08006) and log in now, and each turns red when its own select (`serve_socket`, `serve_held`, the login of `run_session`) goes back to `actions.changed()`. The pool (`tests/sql.rs`, the double has a second password for a reset): a session is pooled across a later route revision, and after the generation moves on the same unit (and the double's password is rotated) the old password is refused with 28P01 instead of being served from the pool, the old session ends, and the new password logs in once and is pooled at the new generation; with the generation check removed it answers 200 for the reset password. **A refusal that was reported as a failed connection.** `authenticate` mapped every guard error of the write of the StartupMessage to 08006 (`sql_stages` outcome `postgres_error`), so a quiesce, a sleep or a replaced unit that began between `open`'s `dialable` check and that guarded write answered 400 with 08006 (a failed connection) and the logged outcome `postgres_error`, although the database was not accepting and nothing had been written. The integrators' published policy (`integrator-handover.md` 3.4) retries 57P03, 08006 and 53300 alike with backoff, so the old answer was retried too: what the change fixes is the meaning of the code (not accepting, nothing written, against a connection that failed) and the logged outcome (`fenced` against `postgres_error`), not whether the client retries (found by the independent verification). `Guard::Fenced` is now 57P03 (outcome `fenced`) there as in `execute`, and `Guard::Lost`, a write that may have reached PostgreSQL, stays 08006. Failing first (`tests/sql.rs`, the same fair-lock method: the request's admission read and its `dialable` read are let through in turn and the entry is published as quiescing behind the second): the request answered 400 with 08006 and the logged outcome `postgres_error`, and answers 400 with 57P03 now, with no StartupMessage at the double; the gateway README says only what that code does. Guards that were green before and stay green: an HTTP request whose database quiesces during its login writes no statement (nothing starting with `parse:` reaches the double), the published quiesce, the replaced unit and the restarted unit tests of `tests/transport.rs`. That was wrong: the admission's read waits for the table's lock (`admit_route`), and tokio's lock is fair, so a writer that queues behind the first read goes ahead of the second. The helper `after_next_read` (`tests/transport.rs`, `tests/sql.rs`) holds the table's write lock, lets the reader that waits behind it through (a failing `try_write` proves that read was granted, since nothing else reads the fixture's table) and returns the writer that queued behind that read; the test then writes the claim's entry (the same unit, generation and operation under route revision 20; the release was under 19) before the next read. Four tests, each for one place that admits a ticket: a v5 ticket the table released at once on the WebSocket path, a held WebSocket wake (the claim lands behind its `wake_state` read, before the admission), an HTTP request released at once and a held HTTP request; each connects or answers 200. One of them also shows a wake the agent refused `desired_stale`; a refused wake is answered `wake_refused` and never `fenced`, so this fault does not explain that one and it stays open. **Look for in the logs of that re-run:** `route_stale` on the first warm requests after a wake. A v6 route the Edge signs right after a wake can name the claim's route revision before the agent has applied the page that carries the claim, and `Gateway::admit` demands the signed revision exactly, so such a route is refused `route_stale`: the same race in the other direction. That disk answers requests in parallel, which EU1's disk has not been shown to do, so the "after" times below are what the code does on a disk that does. **Causes, with the time each cost in the lab on the old code.** (1) `Units::state` was asked for all databases at once (`Core::apply` starts a decision for each, `Units::running` joins them): 300 reads at once failed 260 of them with `org.freedesktop.DBus.Error.LimitsExceeded`, because dbus-daemon allows a connection 128 calls that are not answered yet (`max_replies_per_connection`) and a read is five calls; the failures were the `units_bus` events, retried after 1 s, 2 s, 4 s and so on (915 of them in a start; 2,468 reads in all, 196 s summed), and a read of a unit that is not loaded makes systemd load it (3.7 ms each against 0.2 ms to be told it is not loaded). (4) `deliver_credentials` read one credential at a time before the first apply: 300 round trips, 15 s at 40 ms. 25 s for 300 in the agent's test), so the process, and with it the start of the next agent, waited for them. **Fix.** `Units` lets 16 calls run at once (`CALLS_IN_FLIGHT`, 80 calls at most; the lab refuses past 26 reads, 128 calls), the reads of a unit's state and its property changes alike, so that the CPU quota which `adopt_running` applies at once to every unit it finds running (row `cpu-boost`) cannot flood the bus either and asks `GetUnit` first, so an unloaded unit is inactive without being loaded; | The agent's start reads its two credentials at the same time, and the Worker's read of the node's credentials asks Cloudflare in two rounds when nothing has to change (a Tunnel to create or a record to correct adds a call within its own branch), on branch `start-credentials` (2026-10-20) | **Measured** (EU1, 2026-10-20, main `2f9901b3`, the `agent_start_phase` events of two restarts): the first page at about 1.4 to 1.6 s, `archive_credentials` at 3.0 to 4.2 s and `node_credentials` at 4.1 to 4.4 s (`at_ms`), then `apply`, `settled`, `gateway_table` and `service_started` at 9.1 to 9.7 s; the agent served no wake in that time. **Cause, from the code.** `pull_page` read the archive credentials of the databases (`deliver_credentials`, one request each, 8 at a time) and only then the node's own (`apply_credentials`: the Tunnel token and the route keyring, then the shell's key, the gateway's environment file, the encrypted Tunnel credential and the start of `pgcf-gateway` and `pgcf-cloudflared`). The two share nothing: the first writes `Service::delivered` and the credential store and endpoints of the core (`Core::deliver`), which the archive socket and the jobs read; the second writes `Service::credentials` (the applied revision and the digest of the gateway's secrets), the shell CA file, the gateway's environment file, the Tunnel credential and two units, and needs no archive credential; a restart of the gateway ends no archive read. What needs the archive credentials is `Core::apply` (a restore or a backup job runs with one), so it still runs after both reads; nothing in it was found to need the node's credentials, which the gateway's table does not either (it is served after `settled`), but that is not changed here. **Change.** `tokio::join!` of the two, then one phase `credentials` (the phases `archive_credentials` and `node_credentials` are gone from `agent_start_phase`, `infra/node-image/README.md` says so). The Worker side: `ensureNodeTunnel` (`GET /node/v1/credentials`) made six calls to Cloudflare's API in a row on every read (list the Tunnel, put its configuration, read the DNS record of the gateway, of the shell and of the former shell name, read the token); all but the first need only the Tunnel's identifier, so the first is awaited and the other five are asked at once (`together`: it returns when every call has ended, so that a failed read leaves none running, and the failure is the first in the order of the calls). The calls, their bodies and the checks are the same, no secret is kept (the token is read from Cloudflare on every call), and a Worker keeps six calls open at once, which five do not exceed. **What the archive credential costs the Worker.** `GET /node/v1/archive-credentials/{id}` makes no call to Cloudflare (the Open row said it did): the node lookup and the credential's row are two reads of D1, and the temporary R2 credential is one HMAC signed with the parent key in the Worker (`deliverArchiveCredential`, `signR2Credential`). At 167 volumes and 8 at a time that is 21 rounds, which the 3.0 to 4.2 s of `archive_credentials` fit at about 70 to 130 ms a round (derived from the `at_ms` values, not measured by request). **Tests (failing first).** Agent: `the_archive_credentials_and_the_nodes_credentials_are_read_at_the_same_time` (the link's double answers 8 archive credentials in 600 ms, one round, and the node's credentials in 1,200 ms; in a row the phases `archive_credentials` and `node_credentials` ended at 0.62 s and 1.83 s, the sum of both, and the start took 1.94 s; after the change the phase `credentials` ends at 1.22 s, the longer of the two, and the test asserts 1.2 s up to 1.6 s; the credentials are applied once and every store is there). Worker: `asks Cloudflare for the configuration, the DNS records and the token at the same time once it has the Tunnel` (the double of Cloudflare's API holds every call for 10 ms: 1 call in flight at most before, 5 after, with the shell on and off, and the same records and configuration as before) and `does not fail while a call it made is still running` (with a plain `Promise.all` 4 calls were still running when the read failed). **Expected after a deploy of the API and of the agent, to be measured live:** `first_page`, `units_read`, then one `credentials` ending at about the longer of the two reads, which is the archive credentials when 167 requests of about 100 ms in rounds of 8 are longer than a read of the node's credentials of two Cloudflare round trips; so `service_started` earlier by about the time of the shorter read (the `node_credentials` of 0.2 to 1.1 s), and the rest of the start unchanged. |
