| Keep-warm of the DatabaseActors built on branch `actor-warm` (2026-10-20; D14 part b, owner go 2026-10-20), deployed to Dev 2026-10-20 19:08 UTC; the live pass and its change are the last paragraph | **Design.** `DatabaseActor.warm()` is a new no-op RPC: no SQLite row, D1 statement, counter, presence, clock or ticket, and no table created. `ActorWarmer` (`apps/api/src/actor-warmer.ts`, a new SQLite-backed class, binding `ACTOR_WARMER`, migration tag `v7`) is one Durable Object per shard of 250 live databases on average at the first deploy (78 since the live pass below) (a database is live when neither it nor its project is deleted). A shard is a range of the database ID space: an ID is 20 random characters, a letter and then letters and digits, so the warmer k of n visits the IDs after the first three characters at k/n of the space, up to those at (k+1)/n (the first has no lower end, the last no upper end), which hold 250 databases give or take 6 % and follow each other with no gap and no overlap for any n; a database stays in its shard while the shard count holds. Each warmer runs an alarm loop that sets its next alarm before it works, and each cycle visits its shard's databases in id order with 16 calls at a time at the first deploy (6 since the live pass below) and a 3 s timeout per visit, through the same `databaseActor()` the cron uses (same namespace, `idFromName(database id)`, `DATABASE_ACTOR_LOCATION_HINT`; the warmers carry the hint too), reads only its own range of the primary key's index from D1 (keyset pages of 1,000, so one query for a shard) at most once per 60 s, which with an 8 s interval is every 64 s (and keeps the last list when D1 cannot be read), and writes one log line per cycle (`actor_warm_cycle`: shard, shards, databases, visited, failed, cycle_ms, interval_ms, overrun, list_error). A failed or timed-out visit is counted and never stops the cycle or touches an admission. The minute cron's new step `actor_warmers` (own failure boundary, after `database_actors`) counts the live databases, arms warmer 0 to n-1 (idempotent, one alarm each, a three-minute lease renewed every minute), so an alarm lost to a deploy or a fault is back within a minute, and a warmer the cron stops arming (interval 0, fewer shards) stops itself within three minutes. `DATABASE_ACTOR_WARM_INTERVAL_MS`: unset 8000, 0 off, otherwise 1000 to 300000, anything else fails the step. What every cold Durable Object evaluates grows by the `ActorWarmer` class alone, 772 bytes minified (it imports only `DurableObject`); the cycle (2.6 KB minified) loads with the first alarm and the arming with the cron. **Limits assumed** (Cloudflare's documentation for Workers Paid, which the account runs on): an alarm may run 15 min of wall time and 30 s of CPU; an invocation may make 10,000 subrequests (the first design's shards of 250 made about 250 calls plus one D1 page at each list read; the Workers limits page, read 2026-10-20, lists 50 subrequests on Free and 10,000 on Paid, configurable up to 10 million, and no 1,000, so the claim of staying under an older 1,000 is dropped: a shard is 78 at the default 8 s and 3,000 at the longest interval, 300 s, under 10,000; the page does not say whether calls to Durable Object stubs count); the six-connection limit is listed for fetch, KV, Cache, R2, Queues and TCP and not for Durable Object calls, and the repository already runs 8 actor calls at once (superseded by the live pass below: the Durable Objects limits page lists 6 simultaneous outgoing connections for Durable Objects) (if the runtime queued calls beyond six, the visits would wait, not fail, and `cycle_ms` and `overrun` would show it). The limits pages were read on 2026-10-20: alarm handler 15 min wall time, 30 s CPU, 10,000 subrequests on Workers Paid. A shard of 250 warm actors takes about a second a cycle (an estimate from 50 ms a visit), one of cold actors about 10 s, once, after a deploy; `overrun` says when a cycle outlasts its interval. **Cost model of the first design** (shards of 250, 16 visits in flight, 50 ms a visit; the warmers' line is corrected in the paragraph "A third independent verification" below, and the operator documentation holds the current table; an estimate from the measured rows above at the pricing page of 2026-10-18, not an invoice), per 1,000 databases and month at 8 s: 324 million actor requests USD 48.6, about USD 5 duration, the warmers about USD 4 (about USD 1 per shard, four shards; USD 3.3 under the corrected model), D1 167 million rows read (USD 0.17 gross; 43,200 x 2L + 40,500 x (2L + X) rows a month for L live and X deleted databases, 167,400 per live database; 10.4 billion at 50,000 live and 50,000 deleted databases, against 25 billion included), so 48.6 + 5 + 4 + 0.17 = about USD 58 (USD 10 for 170 databases and USD 18 for 300, warmers included; the three totals are the sums of one table in the operator documentation; the measured 10 s and 5 s figures are 43.6 and 83.8). **Workers Logs is not in that figure and not measured:** the API Worker's Workers Logs hold request lines (so invocation logs are on), and Cloudflare's documentation (pages read 2026-10-20) lists RPC and alarm calls among the handlers that produce one invocation log each, which would be 324 million events per 1,000 databases and month for the visits and 2.6 million for the four warmers (each alarm is an invocation event and each cycle line another: 648,000 a warmer), 326.6 million in all, USD 196 gross at USD 0.60 per million (USD 33 gross for 170 databases, USD 59 for 300), so up to about USD 254 per 1,000 databases (USD 44 for 170, USD 77 for 300); from 2026-12-01 Cloudflare bills logs by volume (USD 0.25 per GB beyond 50 GB: USD 82 gross per 1,000 databases for each kilobyte an event holds). Before the costed go for the deploy, the operator reads the account's Workers Logs usage and the `DatabaseActor` RPC events of the last hour (the cron and the Edge already call the actors), and either accepts the line or sets `observability.logs.invocation_logs` to `false` (a key of the pinned wrangler's schema; it keeps the console lines and drops the request lines) in the private API configuration; the procedure is in the operator documentation. **Tests** (17 new, real workerd, D1 and Durable Objects; red first): `actor-warm-visit.test.ts` (3; red: the RPC receiver did not implement `warm`) compares every row and the in-memory admission state of the Actor, D1's database, epoch and operation rows and the admission answer before and after visits of an awake database, a sleeping one with an issued and claimed wake ticket, and an Actor that holds nothing (it stays without tables and D1 is not read); `actor-warmer.test.ts` (14; red: the module did not exist) covers the ID ranges (contiguous, increasing, no gap or overlap at the boundaries for 2 to 200 shards, even spread of 7,000 and 20,000 random IDs), a cycle that visits exactly the databases of its shard once within the interval and logs one line, the list's time to live and a deleted database or project leaving the list, a failing and a hanging visit not stopping the cycle, a failing D1 read, the namespace, name and location hint, one warmer per shard size with its lease, interval 0 and the invalid values, the cron re-arming a shard whose alarm is gone and reporting a missing binding as the step `actor_warmers`, the alarm setting its next alarm first and surviving a failing cycle, and a lapsed lease stopping the loop. **Independent verification of the first commit found four things, fixed on this branch (a second verification, on the cost sums, is the paragraph after them).** (1) The list read grew with the square of the databases: every warmer paged through all live databases and kept its own by hash, so about 346 N² rows a month, past the 25 billion included near 8,500 databases; now each warmer reads its own ID range (43,200 x 2L + 40,500 x (2L + X) rows a month for the cron's count and the lists together, L live and X deleted databases, 167,400 per live database and 167 million per 1,000 live ones; the cron's count alone is 43,200 x 2L), proved by a test that sums the `rows_read` of the list statements of 2, 3 and 5 warmers over 8 databases (one deleted) against one warmer (15 rows; red before the fix: 30 rows for 2 warmers) and reads the query plan (a search of `sqlite_autoindex_databases_1`, no scan). (2) The loop's continuation and the paging were never run: a cycle now runs with 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 and 16 workers over 7 databases and with a list page of 2 over 5 (3 queries); six mutants of the code are killed on workerd (`index = ++next`; return after the first page; the next page starting at the second-to-last ID; the upper end of a range dropped; the whole table listed by every warmer; and the lease kept), where the first two and the lease had left every test green. (3) The lease renewal test now arms twice 30 ms apart and requires the later lease. (4) The Workers Logs line above. **A second independent verification found the cost sums wrong, fixed on this branch** (the costed go rests on them): the total for 1,000 databases left out two lines of its own table (USD 54 where the lines add to about USD 58, and USD 248 with Workers Logs where they add to about USD 254, which is also the 2.6 million events of the warmers' alarm invocations and cycle lines, 648,000 a warmer and not 324,000), so the three totals disagreed with the USD 10 and USD 18 of the 170- and 300-database figures; the formula was given as 43,200 x 2 x N, which is the cron's count alone, about half of the rows the plan's own 170 million needs. The operator documentation now has one table with the three database counts and the totals as sums of its lines. **Not measured.** A visitor object with an alarm every 8 s over 250 actors (the study's limits) and the visit gap in production: the gap is the interval plus the alarm's jitter plus the spread of a cycle, so the margin below the 10 s edge is about a second; if the live pass finds reloaded actors, lower the interval (5 s costs about USD 84 per 1,000 databases). Expectation for the live pass: see the Open row "Cold gate". **Live pass on Dev and the change it caused, on branch `warmer-place` (2026-10-20, not deployed).** The API Worker was deployed at 19:08 UTC with the interval 8000 ms and one shard of 167 databases. Workers Logs, `actor_warm_cycle`, 19:10 to 19:28 UTC, 109 lines: every cycle visited the whole shard (visited 154 to 167, failed 0 to 13; 83 failed visits in 42 cycles, the 3 s timeout), but `cycle_ms` was 6,714 to 15,203 ms (median 9,024) and `overrun` true in 101 of 109, the gap between two cycle lines 6.7 to 27.2 s (median 9.1 s; twelve gaps of 15 to 27 s); one Edge admission measured right after took 37 ms, so the visits kept the actors warm, but a cycle longer than the 10 s edge of the keep-warm study cannot keep every actor warm. The design had expected about two seconds (50 ms a visit, 16 in flight). 167 visits in 9.0 s are about 320 ms a visit if only six run at once (the limit below applies; 28 rounds) and 820 to 860 ms if all 16 do (10 to 11 rounds). A later read of the same deployment (19:37 to 20:17 UTC, 254 lines at the first read, 255 when re-read at 20:50 UTC) gave a median of 5.9 s (5.4 to 9.6 s, `overrun` in 7): about 210 ms a visit at six at a time or 540 to 570 ms at 16; the fall from 9.0 s is not explained. **Open observation: about 14 % of the cycle lines never arrived.** Re-read at 20:50 UTC with `cf_logs.py` (`actor_warm_cycle` of the one warmer, 167 databases), a cycle's start taken as its log time minus `cycle_ms`: 19:37 to 20:17 has 255 lines where an 8 s loop gives about 299 (15.0 % missing by the clock); 20:17 to 20:40 has 153 where about 172 are expected (11.3 %); the six periods of ten minutes from 19:40 to 20:40 have 67, 63, 63, 62, 68 and 65 lines against 75 (13.8 % missing). From start to start 341 of the 350 gaps under 12 s are 8.00 s (the other 9 are 8.07 to 10.36 s: 8 equal the length of the cycle before, an `overrun`, and one is a late alarm of 8.57 s after a cycle of 5.9 s), and 57 gaps are 16 s or more: 39 in 19:37 to 20:17 (31 of 16.0 s, 3 of 24.0 s, 1 of 32.0 s and 4 of 16.4 to 18.0 s; 44 lines missing, 14.7 % of the 299 cycles) and 18 in 20:17 to 20:40 (17 of 16.0 s, 1 of 24.0 s; 19 lines missing, 11.0 %). 53 of the 57 are a multiple of 8 s to within 7 ms; the other 4 are 0.4 to 2.0 s longer. A gap of exactly k x 8 s counts as k - 1 missing lines and not as a late alarm: the alarm at each multiple fired and set the next alarm before it worked (`alarm()` sets it first), but its cycle line never arrived, so either Workers Logs dropped the line or the alarm ended without completing a cycle (then those actors went 16 to 32 s without a visit, longer than the 10 s a keep-warm needs). The 4 longer gaps are what an unlogged cycle of 8.4 to 10 s leaves (logged cycles overran to 10.4 s), which points at lost lines, but it is no proof for the other 53. The missing starts are spread over the whole minute, so they are not the minute cron's `arm`; there is no `actor_warm_failed` and no `actor_warm_stopped` line from 19:26 to 20:56 UTC, `list_error` is null in all 408 lines and `failed` is above 0 in 41 (a visit given up after 3 s; its line did arrive). 7 of the 67 lines of 19:40 to 19:50 carry `$workers.eventType` `jsrpc` and not `alarm`, so a count of lines must not filter on it. **Open:** which of the two it is, and what it costs a keep-warm that needs a visit every 10 s or faster. **Documentation read 2026-10-20.** The Durable Objects limits page (`https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/limits/`) lists "Simultaneous outgoing connections/request: 6 (same as Workers)" for SQLite-backed and key-value Durable Objects alike; the Workers limits page (`https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/`) says a seventh connection waiting for response headers is queued until one of the six gets them, lists fetch, KV, Cache, R2, Queues and TCP among those counted, says Workers triggered through service bindings share the limit, and does not mention Durable Object stubs. The first design assumed Durable Object calls were exempt (above). The Durable Objects page lists the limit for Durable Objects without saying which calls count, and defers to the Workers rule, whose list does not name stubs (both pages re-read 2026-10-20), so whether a stub call counts is open. The code keeps six calls in flight, which never wait in the runtime's queue under either reading, so `visit_p50_ms` is the call's own time. The shard size holds under both readings only while a visit is short: if stubs are not counted, the 9.0 s at 16 in flight are 820 to 860 ms a visit, and six in flight take 8.2 to 8.6 s for Dev's shards of 56 (10 rounds) and 10.7 to 11.2 s for a full shard of 78 (13 rounds), which is more than the 8 s interval. A full shard of 78 fits the interval at six in flight up to 615 ms a visit (8 s over 13 rounds) and the planned half of it up to 307 ms. At 16 in flight a shard of 78 would take about 4 s under both readings (13 rounds of 300 to 320 ms if the limit applies, 5 of 820 to 860 ms if not), but then, if the limit applies, every visit's time would include its wait in the queue and the line could not say how long the call takes; six was kept for that reason, and its price is the dependency above. The cycle line of a shard that does not fit shows `concurrency` 6, `overrun` true, `visit_p50_ms` above about 600 ms and `cycle_ms` near `ceil(databases / 6) x visit_p50_ms`; the two releases that answer it are in the operator documentation ("Observing it"). **Three hypotheses, none assumed.** (a) The warmer is far from the actors: the minute cron created it by `arm()` wherever that invocation ran, with a hint only if `DATABASE_ACTOR_LOCATION_HINT` was set, while the Edge's admissions run in Amsterdam or London at 37 to 50 ms; a hint places only a new object. (b) The 16 calls in flight queue behind the six-connection limit, so each visit's time includes its wait. (c) A visit does more than one round trip; the code makes one call per stub (`idFromName`, `get` and one RPC; `warm()` is empty), so (c) is not expected. **Changed.** (1) The cycle line gains `concurrency`, `visit_p50_ms` and `visit_max_ms` (a failed visit counts with the time it took; null for a cycle that visited nothing), and each warmer object logs `actor_warmer_placed` once (`shard`, `shards`, `colo` from the `colo` field of `https://www.cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace`, nothing else of the trace, null after 2 s without an answer, and `new_warmer_location_hint`, the hint that the variables give a warmer created now); with six in flight no visit waits in the runtime's queue, so `visit_p50_ms` is the call itself and the colo separates (a) from (b). (2) Warmers are placed with `DATABASE_ACTOR_LOCATION_HINT` if set, else with the new variable `ACTOR_WARMER_LOCATION_HINT` (Dev: `weur`), and named `v2:<shard>` (constant `ACTOR_WARMER_NAME_VERSION`) because a hint places only a new object; the warmers of the earlier name `shard-<n>` are not armed any more, their lease (three minutes) runs out, their next alarm logs `actor_warm_stopped`, sets no alarm and deletes the stored shape (a test arms one of the earlier name, lets the cron arm the new ones and watches it stop). (3) 6 visits in flight (`ACTOR_WARM_CONCURRENCY`) and a shard of `floor(interval x 0.5 / 300 ms)` rounds of six visits, 78 databases at 8 s (13 rounds, 3.9 s planned, half the interval; a shard of twice the average still ends within the interval); the 300 ms (`ACTOR_WARM_VISIT_PLAN_MS`) is the figure the live cycles imply if the limit applies (320 ms; 820 to 860 ms if not) and is to be lowered to the `visit_p50_ms` of a read taken with the warmers placed near the actors. Dev's 167 databases are three warmers of about 56 databases (9 or 10 rounds, about 3 s at 300 ms, about 0.5 s at 50 ms); the warmers cost about USD 28 more per 1,000 databases and month than shards of 250 (USD 31.2 at 300 ms a visit against 3.3; the paragraph "A third independent verification" below and the operator documentation hold the model and the table: about USD 85 per 1,000 databases without Workers Logs and up to about USD 284 with them, USD 15 and USD 49 for 170). **Tests**, real workerd, red first (the 25 of `actor-warmer.test.ts` after the third verification, below; 11 were red before the change, for the reasons below): the new cycle-line fields and the null of an empty shard; at most six visits in flight over 8 databases (peak 6; was 8); the median and the longest visit with delays of 40, 160 and 400 ms and a timed-out visit counted; the warmer names (`v2:0`, was `shard-0`); the hint of the warmer from `ACTOR_WARMER_LOCATION_HINT`, the actors' hint taking precedence, and none; a warmer of the earlier name not renewed by the cron, then stopping with no alarm and nothing stored (red before: the cron renewed its lease); one `actor_warmer_placed` line per warmer object over two alarms with only the colo logged out of a trace that holds an address; the line with the hint, with no colo when the trace fails, has no colo or never answers (given up within 3.5 s); the shard size for five intervals (a whole number of rounds, at most half the interval, the largest that fits) and the arming of two warmers for 11 databases at 1 s. **An independent verification of this commit found three things, fixed on this branch.** (1) The cycle test failed about one run in five (its four random database IDs left shard 0 of 3 empty with probability (2/3)^4, about 20 %, and an empty shard's visit times are null by design while the test expected numbers): red, 3 of 15 isolated runs; now each line is judged by the size of its own shard (null when it is 0) and the test passed in 25 of 25 isolated runs. (2) The fallback claim above was false by the commit's own numbers ("also correct if stubs are not counted" and "the Durable Objects page contradicts that"); corrected above, with the signature that shows it. (3) The cost text said "one warmer for every 250 databases" for the table of shards of 78 and "USD 9 more in warmers and their log events", where the table's own lines are USD 9.0 more for the warmers and USD 3.5 more for the log events, USD 12.5 with Workers Logs (the warmers' line itself was wrong, corrected in the next paragraph). **A third independent verification found three things, fixed on this branch.** (1) The warmers' cost basis was the first design's (250 databases a shard, 16 visits in flight, 50 ms a visit, about a second a cycle, about USD 1 a warmer), but this branch sizes a shard so that a cycle takes half the interval at 300 ms a visit (3.9 s for 78 databases, 3.0 s for Dev's 56), and a Durable Object's duration is wall-clock time while it is active, waiting for the actors included (pricing page: "Durable Objects are billed for compute duration (wall-clock time)"; limits page: "Durable Objects remain active while a request, RPC call, response stream, WebSocket, or pending I/O is in flight"; both read 2026-10-20). The line is now modelled per warmer and month as requests USD 0.06 + rows written USD 0.37 + 0.506 x cycle seconds (USD 0.42 fixed): USD 1.94 for a shard of 57 databases (3.0 s) and USD 2.40 for 75 to 77 (3.9 s). At the planned 300 ms the warmers cost USD 5.8, 9.6 and 31.2 for 170, 300 and 1,000 databases (the table said 3.0, 4.0 and 13.0), the totals are about USD 15, 26 and 85 without Workers Logs and 49, 86 and 284 with them (the table said 12, 20 and 67, and 46, 80 and 266), and shards of 78 cost about USD 28 more in warmers per 1,000 databases than shards of 250 (3.3 at 16 in flight and 50 ms a visit), USD 31 with the log events, not USD 9 and 12.5. At the 50 ms the first design expected the warmers cost 2.0, 3.0 and 9.8 and the totals are about 11, 19 and 64. The warmers' duration is about databases / concurrency x visit time: it falls with the visit time, not with the number of warmers (a warmer more adds USD 0.42), and six in flight instead of 16 cost up to 2.7 times the duration if stub calls do not count against the six connections, and 1.9 times once the cap is applied (USD 53 against 28 of the warmers' 57 and 33 per 1,000 databases, at 840 ms a visit). **Corrected after a fourth independent verification:** the cycles of 8.4 s (shards of 57) and 10.9 s (75 to 77) at six in flight are longer than the interval, so each alarm starts when the one before has ended and a warmer is active at most the whole month, which caps its duration at 2,592,000 s x 0.125 GB x USD 12.50 per million GB-s = USD 4.05 a warmer; the first figures (14.0, 23.8 and 77.4, 2.7 times, USD 72) counted such cycles 324,000 times a month, which a month cannot hold. With the cap, and 308,571 and 237,798 cycles a month for the requests and the rows written, the warmers cost 13.4, 17.5 and 56.9 for 170, 300 and 1,000 databases (USD 53 of the 56.9 is duration: 13 warmers x 4.05), and the first read's 9.0 s median is USD 4.4 a month for that warmer (the operator documentation had 5.0). Live Dev (one warmer, 167 databases, 16 in flight) ran a median cycle of 5.9 s in 254 cycle lines (2026-10-20 19:37 to 20:17 UTC; 255 when re-read, where an 8 s loop gives about 299, see the open observation above), USD 3.4 a month for that warmer. (2) The test "a trace that never answers is given up on" did not prove the timeout: its fetch double read `init.signal.addEventListener` unguarded, so with no signal it threw at once and rejected instead of hanging, and the mutant that removes `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(...)` left all 24 tests green. The double now settles only when its own signal aborts, the case is its own test and races the call against 3.5 s, and the mutant fails it ("held") while the code passes it. The timeout matters because alarms do not overlap: a trace that hangs would hold the first cycle of its warmer and every visit after it. (3) The `actor_warmer_placed` field `location_hint` was the hint the current variables give a warmer created now, not the hint the object was placed with (a hint applies only when an object is created): after a deploy with `ACTOR_WARMER_LOCATION_HINT=weur` the line of the earlier warmer `shard-0`, created without a hint, would have shown `location_hint: "weur"`, which is false for it. The field is renamed `new_warmer_location_hint` and documented as that; for a warmer created earlier only `colo` says where it runs. **Not measured.** The warmer's colo and the visit time near the actors (the next read), and whether Durable Object stubs are counted against the six connections (a read at six in flight shows the call's own time under both readings and does not decide it), and why about 14 % of the cycle lines never arrived (the open observation above). **Next live read, after deploying with `ACTOR_WARMER_LOCATION_HINT` set (Dev: `weur`)** and 4 to 5 minutes (the minute cron creates `v2:0` to `v2:2`; the earlier warmer stops after its lease): `actor_warmer_placed` for `shards` 3 with a colo in West Europe and `new_warmer_location_hint` `weur` (and one for `shards` 1, the earlier warmer, which was created without a hint: its `colo` is where it has run in all along and decides between (a) and (b), while its `new_warmer_location_hint` also reads `weur`, because that field is the setting for new warmers and not the hint the object was placed with); `actor_warm_cycle` for `shards` 3 with `databases` about 56, `visited` equal to `databases`, `failed` 0, `overrun` false, `concurrency` 6, `visit_p50_ms` below 100 (expected 40 to 60) and `cycle_ms` about `ceil(databases / 6) x visit_p50_ms` (under 1.5 s), the gap from start to start (log time minus `cycle_ms`) of a shard's cycle lines 8.0 to 8.3 s, a gap of exactly k x 8 s counting as k - 1 missing lines and not as a late alarm, and the count of lines of each shard over ten minutes, 75 expected at 8 s (count without a filter on `$workers.eventType`): a shard with fewer lines whose lines show `overrun` true and gaps equal to their `cycle_ms` is slow (placement or the visit time), one with fewer lines, `overrun` false and gaps of exact multiples of 8 s has lost lines or alarms, and a loss in every shard and not in one points at Workers Logs and not at a warmer's place; one `actor_warm_stopped` with `shard` 0 within about 3.5 minutes of the deploy; the Edge's `admit_ms` of a first connect after a quiet period 40 to 80 ms; the cost model then reads off the median `cycle_ms` of each shard (USD 0.42 + 0.506 per second a month: about 0.5 s and USD 0.7 at 50 ms a visit, 3.0 s and USD 1.9 at the planned 300 ms). Up to a `visit_p50_ms` of 615 ms a shard of 78 still fits the interval, and up to 307 ms it keeps the planned margin of half. If `visit_p50_ms` stays above about 600 ms with a colo in West Europe and `overrun` true, the call itself is slow near the actors (at six in flight the six-connection limit is not the cause), the shard size does not hold, and the releases are in the operator documentation ("Observing it"). |

| Restore into a smaller class, on branch `pr-w1b` (2026-10-21; built and tested, not deployed) | **Found:** a restore or PITR of a backup taken in a class with more `max_connections` than the target (catalog: xs 20, sm 100, md 200, lg 300) aborted with "recovery aborted because of insufficient parameter settings"; the fixed `max_worker_processes = 8` and `max_wal_senders = 10` of the recovery covered two of the five settings PostgreSQL 18.6 compares. **Built:** the agent reads `max_connections`, `max_worker_processes`, `max_wal_senders`, `max_prepared_transactions` and `max_locks_per_transaction` from the restored backup's `pg_control` (offsets 180 to 196, checked against PostgreSQL 18.6 files), runs the recovery with the larger of each and the class's, refuses it with `build_failed` before the start when the shared memory of those settings is more than half of the class's `memory.max`, and restarts the database onto the class's settings (it stays admitted) before the first base backup, only when the recovery ran with more. **Measured (PostgreSQL 18.6, `postgres -C shared_memory_size`):** about 49 KiB of shared memory per connection slot at the default 64 locks (20 connections 22 MB, 200 connections 31 MB, 10,000 connections 509 MB, each with 16 MB of buffers); about 0.4 KiB per lock per slot; the buffers cost 2.6 % (16 GiB) to 12.5 % (16 MiB) more than their size. The model in `settings.rs` stays 1.0 to 1.5 times the server's figure over the grid of buffer sizes from 8 MiB to 16 GiB and 20 to 10,000 connections. **Tests (real PostgreSQL 18.6, Alpine 3.24 container, non-root, `restore.rs`, `postgres_tests.rs`, `apply.rs`):** red first (`start_failed`, the startup process dying with "max_connections = 20 is a lower setting than on the primary server, where its value was 200"), then green for restore and PITR of a source with 200 connections, 10 workers, 12 senders, 4 prepared transactions and 128 locks into xs: promoted, the same digest (md5 of the rows) as the source at the end and at the target time, one restart, `SHOW` giving the class's 20 / 4 / 0 / 0 / 64; the same through the real core and unit start (`Rebuild::restart`), where the writer is the restarted postmaster; without the restart both fail on `max_connections` 200. **A source resized up and down again between its backup and the restore** (found by the independent check, reproduced against PostgreSQL 18.6): the WAL carries a parameter change above the backup's settings and the class's, PostgreSQL pauses the recovery with "recovery has paused" while its postmaster reports `ready`, and `Rebuild::promoted` polled `pg_is_in_recovery` with no end, so the restore stayed in `Building` and admitted for good. Now `promoted` reads `pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state()` too and fails with `no_recovery_point`, and the database is abandoned (`apply.rs`, real core and unit start, source resized 25 to 200 to 25 connections: red first, the restore still `Building` after 60 s with "max_connections = 25 is a lower setting than on the primary server, where its value was 200" in the log; green: phase `Error`, `no_recovery_point`, unit stopped, volume gone). Such a restore is refused, not served: reading the WAL ahead for the values is built only if a live restore needs it. **Left:** the live check on the current image (restore and PITR of an md database into xs, `restore_phase` `restarted`, create to ready of the restore) |
| A failed wake returns the idle sleeper to its idle sleep, built on branch `pr-w1c` (2026-10-20), not deployed | **Cause.** A `database.wake` is the claim of a connection's ticket: D1 goes to `running` at the next generation with a pending wake, and the node starts the database through the gateway's wake. Nothing in D1 ended a wake that did not end in a running database. The agent reports such a wake as `asleep` at the wake's generation, not as an error: a ticket it refuses, a start that fails or a restart of the agent during the wake leaves the unit asleep (`after_failed_start` in `power.rs` sets `Phase::Asleep`), and `start_failed` is only a build's or a restore's error. D1 then showed the database desired running and observed `provisioning` (asleep) with a wake that nothing carries out; the 20-minute power timeout named `database.resume` alone, so the generic sweep only failed the pending wake, and the Actor's snapshot no longer said wakeable. **Change.** `recoverFailedResume` (`lifecycle.ts`) takes a pending or running `database.wake` as it takes a `database.resume`: the operation fails with the reason, and a database that D1 knows asleep is suspended again at the next generation as its last suspension was, which for a wake is always the idle hibernation (status message `Wake failed: <reason>`). The caller for a wake is the cron's power timeout (`undoneByPowerTimeout` in `cron.ts` names `database.wake` beside `database.resume`, and so the generic sweep leaves a timed-out wake to it): the wake fails with `operation_timeout` 20 minutes after its last update. The node then pulls the suspended entry and proves the sleep again; its `asleep` report ends the new hibernation and writes the `hibernated` event, and the next connection gets a new ticket. A suspension that is not proven in 20 minutes is only failed, not turned into a wake again, as before (a database D1 knows asleep needs no undo). **Not changed.** `database.resume` (its order result and its timeout), `database-actor.ts`, `node-observations.ts`, and every `error` observation. A wake ended by a persistent node error (`volume_missing`, `identity_mismatch`) is not returned to sleep: the observation fails the wake, the database stays `running` / `error`, and the next connections reuse the ticket at the same generation with no D1 write, as before. A first build of this branch also returned the sleeper to sleep for an `error` observation of a wake; probed on real D1 and Durable Objects with `volume_missing` it claimed a new wake and a new hibernation at every connection (generation 3 to 10 in three connections, `observed_state` back from `error` to `provisioning`), and the agent sends no such error for a wake, so that branch was removed. **Tests, failing first** (`apps/api/test/domain/failed-wake-sleep.test.ts`, real D1 and Durable Object harness, a sleeper woken through `admitWake` and its claim). (1) The node's `asleep` at the wake's generation, a cron run before the wake is 20 minutes old (it leaves the wake to the node), and a cron run 21 minutes after it: the wake is failed with `operation_timeout`, the database is `suspended` / `idle` at generation 4 with a pending `database.hibernate` and the status message `Wake failed: operation_timeout`; then the node's `asleep` at generation 4 ends the hibernation with the `hibernated` event and the proven sleep, and `admitWake` issues a new ticket for generation 5 that the node's ready report ends. (2) The same return to sleep, whose hibernation the node does not prove: a cron run 21 minutes later fails the hibernation with `operation_timeout` and leaves the database `suspended` / `idle` at generation 4. (3) A wake ended by a `volume_missing` observation: the wake is failed with `volume_missing`, the database stays `running` / `error` at generation 3, `admitWake` reuses the ticket of generation 3, and a cron run 21 minutes later changes nothing. Tests 1 and 2 failed first on the state (`running`, generation 3, no hibernation operation) with the cron and lifecycle changes taken out; test 3 passes without the change too and holds the claim that a persistent error is not returned to sleep. The whole API suite passes (110 files, 1059 tests). **Boundary.** A ticket wake the node refuses is no result to D1, and the node's `asleep` at the wake's generation does not return the sleeper sooner: the next connection reuses the ticket (which works, as found) or, if none comes, the database returns to sleep after the 20 minutes. Open row "A failed wake leaves D1 at `running` / `provisioning`". |
| The gateway drains on a release swap and hands its socket over, on branch `gateway-drain-proof` (2026-10-21; closes the code part of S3-03, G2), built and tested, not deployed; a second and a third round fixed the findings of the independent verification (second: the new gateway accepted before it had the agent's table; third: the outcome of work cut at the bound, and the order of the first release's restarts) | **Before.** On SIGTERM `main.rs` stopped accepting but kept the listening socket, so a new connection completed its handshake and was never answered until the process exited and reset it; every established WebSocket kept its place for 29 s, also an idle one, so the old process lived 29 to 30 s and `Restart=always` could bind only after it (a gap of up to 30 s for new connections, longer than the integrators' retry rule of 1, 2, 4 and 8 s); a session still busy at 29 s was closed with code 1012 and no SQLSTATE; an HTTP `/sql` request still running at 30 s was aborted with no answer, which the Edge reports as its own `08007` ("the gateway's answer was lost"), so the client could not tell a request that ran from one that never started; `/healthz` answered `ok` while draining; a request read after the drain began got `57P03` (HTTP) or `fenced` (WebSocket). **Built.** (1) `transport::serve` is the accept loop and the drain, moved out of `main.rs` so that tests drive the same code (`Gateway::drain(bound)` replaces the flag; `DRAIN_BOUND` is 10 s). (2) The drain closes a session that is not busy at once with code 1012 and a busy one as soon as it is idle (the test that closes a sleeping database's idle sessions), so a transaction that commits is kept. (3) A session still busy at the bound is told what became of it and closed (no error is inserted while half a message of PostgreSQL's is on its way, `PostgresActivity::backend_partial`). **A session idle in a transaction** gets a FATAL `57P01`; ending the connection ends the transaction, so it is rolled back. **A session with a statement in flight** (`PostgresActivity::in_flight`: a whole request not yet answered through ReadyForQuery, an extended sequence, COPY, or anything the observer cannot follow) gets a FATAL `08007` (transaction_resolution_unknown), because ending the gateway's connection does not stop PostgreSQL: it finishes the statement and the `COMMIT` the client pipelined behind it and notices the lost client only when it writes its answer, so the work can commit after the error, up to the statement's run time later (third round; the first build sent `57P01` here, which claims a rollback that is not true). An HTTP `/sql` request still running at the bound is answered by the gateway itself, `08007` if its statements were sent (outcome unknown, not retried, and the same: it can commit after the answer) and `08006` otherwise, and the Edge passes a 400 with a code on as it is. A `CancelRequest` with the session's `BackendKeyData` would shorten the window and not close it (PostgreSQL ignores a cancel that arrives between statements, and the `COMMIT` may have run before it arrives), so it would still need the `08007` and is not built. (4) New work is refused with `gateway_draining`: `08006` "gateway restarting" over HTTP (as a held wake already was) and HTTP 503 `gateway_draining` for a WebSocket upgrade; `/healthz` answers `draining` (200) and `/readyz` 503. (5) **The listening socket is systemd's** (`pgcf-gateway.socket`, `ListenStream` on the loopback port the Tunnel's ingress names; `pgcf-gateway.service` requires it, so a release that delivers both files needs no preset; as a host file it gets only the reload, because a restart of the socket stops the gateway; the reload leaves a running socket as it was, which matters for a rollback below). The gateway takes it as descriptor 3 under the `sd_listen_fds` protocol (`activation.rs`: only for the process `LISTEN_PID` names, exactly one socket, loopback only) and binds its own when it has none, so the new binary also runs under the old unit during the release that brings the socket. A connection that arrives while the old gateway drains or before the new one starts waits in the socket's queue and is accepted by the new one; (6) the accept loop takes a handshake slot (128) before it accepts, so the burst that meets the new gateway, every connection that waited, is served in turn and the ones beyond the slots wait in the socket, where the loop used to accept them and drop them with a reset (seen once in the busy swap test under load: "Connection reset by peer"); (7) **the new gateway accepts only with the agent's table** (second round). The first build started `transport::serve` as soon as `main` held the listener, while `local::synchronize` was still connecting to the agent, and `admit_route` answers `fenced` while the table has not arrived, so the connections that had waited in the socket were accepted into a refusal: 503 `{"error":"fenced"}`, which the Edge turns into `08006` and a `/sql` request would have got as `57P03`. The swap tests did not see it because their probes were `GET /healthz`, which answers 200 without a table. `serve` now waits for the first table before its accept loop (`Gateway::table_arrived`, bound `FIRST_TABLE_BOUND` of 5 s; the agent sends the table as soon as the gateway connects, so the wait is the time of the connect): the connections keep waiting in the socket, and after the bound the gateway accepts and refuses with `fenced` as it always did without a table, instead of leaving them without an answer; a stop during the wait drains at once. **Tests, red first** (`apps/native-gateway/tests/drain.rs`, a real PostgreSQL 18; `activation.rs`; `infra/node-image/gateway-socket.test.ts`). Red on the unchanged drain: a session that committed in the drain was not closed within 2 s (`([], None)`); an idle WebSocket was not closed in 2 s; a session cut at the bound got no error (`([], Some(1012))` against `57P01`); an HTTP request still running at the bound got no answer; `/healthz` said `ok`; with the socket handover disabled the swap test had no answer at all; the 129th connection while 128 handshakes were open was accepted and reset at once. **Second round, red first:** the independent verification measured, with the swap probes changed to real WebSocket upgrades on the first build, 1, 3 and 2 connections of three idle swaps and 7 and 11 connections of two swaps with a transaction open (which had waited 9.5 to 10 s in the socket) refused with 503 `fenced`. The swap tests now probe with upgrades, which pass only if the new gateway admits the route, and three tests drive `serve` with an agent whose table arrives late, never, or after a stop. Red against the first build's `serve` (the new parameter present and unused): both swap tests failed with `status 503: {"error":"fenced"}`, a connection made 0.9 s before the table arrived got 503 `fenced` at once, and one made with no table at all was refused after 6 ms instead of at the bound (the test of the stop passes before and after: it guards the new wait). Green after: a transaction in flight at the start commits, the session then closes with 1012 within 2 s and the serve loop returns within 2 s; an idle WebSocket closes with 1012 within 2 s; a transaction open (idle) at a 1 s bound ends with `57P01` and 1012, and PostgreSQL then has no session left in it and the row never appears; an HTTP transaction in flight at the start (a 1.5 s sleep) commits and is answered; one still running at a 1 s bound is answered `08007` within 3 s while its statement is still running, and the row appears when the statement has ended (the third round's figures are below); new work gets `08006` / 503 `gateway_draining`; a connection that arrives 0.9 s before the table is upgraded when it arrives (it waited at least 0.7 s); one that waits for a table that does not come is refused `fenced` at the bound (0.5 s to 3 s for a bound of 0.6 s); a stop during the wait ends the serve loop within 2 s. **Third round, red first.** The independent verification measured, on a scratch copy with the bound at 1 s and a 4 s sleep, that work cut at the bound is committed afterwards, though the build answered it as ended: an HTTP transaction answered `08007` had 0 rows at the answer and 1 row 6 s later; a WebSocket autocommit `insert ... from pg_sleep(4)` got `57P01` and 1012, and then committed; so did `begin; insert; select pg_sleep(4); commit`. The cause is that the gateway only drops its connection to PostgreSQL, which buffers its results until ReadyForQuery, notices the lost client when it writes, and already holds the `COMMIT` the gateway pipelined. The old assertion (`count = 0` while `pg_sleep(30)` still ran) proved nothing, because an uncommitted row is invisible whether the transaction later rolls back or commits; the idle-in-transaction tests had the same weakness. The tests now wait until PostgreSQL has nothing left to run for the tenant (`settled`: no session running a statement or in a transaction) before they count. **Red** on the second round's code, with the claim it made (the row is rolled back once the statement has ended): the HTTP test counted `1` against `0`; the two WebSocket tests (an autocommit statement, and `begin; insert; select pg_sleep(3); commit` as one request) failed with `(["57P01"], Some(Some(1012)))` against `(["08007"], Some(Some(1012)))`. **Fix:** the smaller of the two ways, to answer what is true instead of settling it: `08007` for a session with a statement in flight (`PostgresActivity::in_flight`), `57P01` only for a session idle in a transaction, and the documents say that the outcome settles when PostgreSQL has finished the statement (`apps/native-gateway/README.md`, `docs/operations/integrator-handover.md` 7.1: repeat only an idempotent write, check a write's effect only after the statement's run time). **Green:** both WebSocket tests get `08007` and 1012 with the statement still running and 0 rows at the error, and the row is there when it ended; the HTTP request is answered `08007` ("outcome is unknown") within 3 s with the same outcome; the idle-in-transaction tests (the single session and the swap with a transaction open) get `57P01` and PostgreSQL then has no session in the transaction and no row. `PostgresActivity::in_flight` has unit tests: half a request is not in flight, a whole one is until ReadyForQuery, an idle-in-transaction and a failed-transaction session are not, an extended sequence, COPY and a message the observer does not know are. `in_flight` is a Rust predicate of the gateway like `backend_partial`; the TypeScript observer and its vectors (`packages/contracts/native`, cold-pc's files) do not have it. **The gap, measured with the real binary** and the socket passed as systemd passes it (descriptor 3, `LISTEN_PID`), the old process sent SIGTERM and the new one started 300 ms after it had exited (`RESTART_GAP`: a restart takes a few milliseconds, too short for more than a few connections to arrive in it, so the test makes the gap one in which many do), new connections that are real WebSocket upgrades every 5 ms (50 ms with a transaction open), none in the 15 ms around the signal (a connection the old gateway had accepted and not yet read when the signal arrived gets the refusal of a draining gateway above, `08006`, and is retried; it is one connection in a window of microseconds and the test of the refusal covers it): with an idle session open, 11 runs of 76 to 87 connections of which 44 to 56 arrived during the swap were all upgraded and the longest waited 300 to 331 ms (the 300 ms gap and the start); with a transaction open, 3 runs of 222 to 223 connections of which 218 to 219 arrived during the swap were all upgraded by the new gateway and the longest waited 10.27 s, which is `DRAIN_BOUND` and the gap and inside the 15 s of the retry rule, and the session got `57P01` and 1012 and was rolled back. The first build's figures (16 ms and 10.03 s) came from probes that the new gateway answered without a table and are replaced by these. **Under systemd** (a privileged Debian 13 container, arm64 on the build Mac, with systemd 257.13 as PID 1, which is the image's version (the image is amd64); the real units and the real binary, built in the pinned builder image, with no agent): `systemctl restart pgcf-gateway` with a request every 50 ms kept the socket unit's invocation, the gateway printed `"inherited":true`, 48 requests were all answered `200`, and the slowest waited 5.05 s, the bound for a table that does not come. The release that brings the socket (a gateway that runs on its own port under the old units, then the new unit files, one reload and `systemctl restart pgcf-gateway`): systemd stopped the gateway, then listened on the socket, then started the gateway, which printed `"inherited":true`; `/healthz` answered 200. **Not seen on a node.** Two live checks, on two releases (L-B2 of the production-readiness plan). The next release that changes the gateway binary is **this** release, and its first gateway swap shows the old gap (up to 30 s, from the old binary): measure it as the one-time outage it is, and the second swap, the shorter drain without a handover; the new behaviour (the handover, the 10 s bound, `08007` and `57P01`) is checked at the release after it, when the gateway binary or the route keys change again. What each check has to see: SQL transactions kept running on three awake test databases, each outcome and SQLSTATE recorded; that cloudflared and the Edge hold a connection that waits up to 10 s in the socket instead of failing it earlier (a waiting connection is not an error, but the Edge's own timeout for the gateway is not read here); that the agent's restart of the unit keeps the socket as `systemctl restart` did in the container (the QEMU boot test of the image is the first run of the units on the image itself); the time the new gateway waits for the agent's first table on the node (the container had no agent); and what a herd of reconnects after the 1012 costs. Limits of the rollout (corrected in the third round): the release that brings the socket restarts the gateway twice, and neither restart is a handover. The agent restarts the gateway right after it has installed the binaries and before it writes the host files (`apps/node-agent/src/service.rs`, `install` and then `host_files`), so **the first restart stops the OLD binary**, which drains with the old code: every WebSocket is held for up to 29 s, also an idle one, and the port is kept without accepting for up to 30 s, then the connections that waited are reset. That is the long gap of critic item 12, once, and it cannot be fixed from here, because it is the old binary's behaviour; it is recorded for the integrators in `docs/operations/integrator-handover.md` (7.1). The new binary starts under the old unit and binds its own port. **The second restart (the host files) stops that new binary**: the shorter drain (idle sessions closed at once, busy ones at most 10 s, the serve loop back after at most 12 s) but no handover, because the process holds its own listening socket: a connection that arrives meanwhile waits in that queue and is reset when the process exits, after which systemd listens on the socket and starts the gateway with it. **The first swap with a handover is the restart of the release after that**, the next one that changes the gateway binary or the route keys. **A rollback and a roll forward, measured** (same container; the old binary is the new one with `LISTEN_PID`, `LISTEN_FDS` and `LISTEN_FDNAMES` unset, which is how a binary older than the socket behaves; the independent verification of the first build found it, and it was repeated here): (a) no operator step is needed. The old binary, restarted by the install under the current units, finds its port held by the socket and exits with status 1 (`gateway_stopped_with_error`: the bind of its own port fails); `Restart=always` starts it again every second (4 exits and 3 scheduled restarts in the 4 s of the run) until the old release's host files are applied. At the reload that removes the socket file systemd logs "Socket unit configuration has changed while unit has been running, no open socket file descriptor left. The socket unit is not functional until restarted." and closes the socket; the next start of the old gateway binds its own port and serves (`/healthz` 200, `"inherited":false`). The crash loop lasts from the install restart to the old release's host files; its length on a node is not measured. (b) Stopping `pgcf-gateway.socket` first, as the first build's text advised, is wrong: it stops the gateway at once (the service requires the socket; `/healthz` gave no answer), and the install restart under the current unit starts the socket again, so the crash loop happens anyway (3 restarts in 4 s). (c) **The handover is lost silently after a roll forward:** with the new binary, the socket file back and one reload, the socket unit stays active without a descriptor, so the new gateway binds its own port (`"inherited":false`) and serves without the handover until the socket is restarted or the node reboots; `systemctl restart pgcf-gateway.socket` stopped and started the gateway and it printed `"inherited":true` again. The same holds for any later release that changes the socket file, because the host file is applied with the reload only (`infra/node-image/host-files.ts`). After such a release the check is the gateway's `gateway_listening` line in the journal: `"inherited":true`. The sentence in `infra/node-image/README.md` that the gateway "is not drained first yet" is cold-sb's file and still says so. |

A region whose nodes are all at the bound therefore gives the purchase signal (the decision answers `adopt` or `order`) and a new database waits as "Waiting for verified regional capacity". `growthFits` refuses storage growth only at the cap, with no reading or with no room, and not for the count, the pool's data or its metadata (a resize creates no volume and takes no real space), and `closedPools` lists the node, so `regional_node_pool_closed` fires for it; the kind's definition and its runbook action in the contract (`INFRA_ALERT_ACTIONS`) and the four documents that define it (`README.md`, the handover, `infrastructure-backups.md`, `recovery.md`) now name the 1,000 volumes next to the pool's data, metadata and cap, with the same `kind` and `node_ids`. **Why 1,000.** It is the largest count Stage 1 measured (4.11), and the bound rises only after a measurement at a higher count. It is not the metadata area: the agent creates a 64 MiB one (`pvcreate --metadatasize 67108864b`), which holds about 95,000 volumes (4.3). Volumes created between two samples are not counted (the newest sample in D1 lags by up to about a minute), so a node can end a little past 1,000. `PEAK_WINDOW_MS` stayed at 7 days then (owner default O6); it is 3 days since 2026-10-23 (11.3). **Purchases, what the code did.** With autoscale on, an order configured and purchases off, `runNodeCapacity` reserved an order addition (a held slot, and the AddNode Workflow polling it for 24 h). Nothing was bought meanwhile, because `claimNodeDispatch` needs `purchases_enabled=1` (and `autoscale_enabled=1` for a capacity order), but the held addition was approved under a standing profile and dispatched by the next pass after purchases were turned on, for a shortage that might be long gone. With autoscale off nothing was reserved (action `disabled`, and the reservation SQL refuses a capacity key). **Now** the cron reserves no order while purchases are off (action `purchases_disabled`, in the dry run as well). The switch is also read by the reservation itself: `automaticAuthoritySql` (`node-state.ts`) requires `purchases_enabled=1` next to `autoscale_enabled=1`, so an operator `PUT` that lands between the cron's policy read and `reserveNodeAddition` reserves nothing (before, that race left a `capacity-headroom-` order reserved with a held slot while purchases were off, `waiting_for_approval`, and the next pass after purchases were turned on approved and dispatched it for a shortage that might be gone; the approval and dispatch statements already required `purchases_enabled=1`, so they do not change). In that race the action reads `purchases_disabled` as well: after `capacity_unavailable` the cron reads the switch again, and answers `cap_reached` only when purchases are on. Adopting an allocated instance, which costs nothing, still goes first, and manual order additions are unchanged. **Tests, red first:** `placement-volume-bound.test.ts` (999 volumes open and 1,000 closed, read through the D1 sample, for create, restore and move; the next node takes the database, with the node at the bound the fuller one so the test fails on every run without the bound; `closedPools`; the capacity decision `idle` at 999 and `adopt` at 1,000, with the addition reserved and AddNode started), `node-capacity.test.ts` (purchases off: `purchases_disabled`, no addition, AddNode not started, one reserved once purchases are on), `standing-node-approval.test.ts` and `node-capacity.test.ts` again for the race (a headroom reservation with purchases off and autoscale on is refused; purchases turned off while the run checks for maintenance end in `purchases_disabled` with no addition and AddNode not started; before the fix the run returned `waiting_for_approval` with an addition reserved) and `placement.test.ts`, "which node takes the storage growth of a database it holds" (one case per combination of the pool's data at 80 %, its metadata at 50 %, the cap and the 1,000 volumes: `growthFits` refuses storage growth exactly when the cap is reached, whatever else has closed the node, and `choosePlacement` takes the node only when nothing has closed it; the four cases that combine the cap with data or metadata, and the growth up to the cap on a node at 80 % of its data, were red before the reorder). **Pinning tests, green before the change:** autoscale off reserves no addition, a resize still fits at the bound, storage growth past four times the pool is still refused at the bound, and a pool with no room (`room: false` at 75 % of its metadata) refuses storage growth but not memory growth, which is why the handover says that only the cap or a pool with no room refuses it; the alert text is tied to the constant in `placement-volume-bound.test.ts` (the definition and the action of `regional_node_pool_closed` name `MAX_VOLUMES_PER_NODE` volumes). The OpenAPI text of `autoscale_enabled` and `purchases_enabled` (`platform/nodes.ts`, the contract) now says the cron reserves an order only while `purchases_enabled` is true. **Left:** deploy with D-1; the bound itself cannot be reached live without 1,000 volumes, so the live check is that EU1 still places (`volumes.total` read from its live sample, the capacity decision `idle`); `operator-installation.md` (cold-e's file, not edited here; DOC-2) still lists the actions without `purchases_disabled`, and its `autoscale_enabled` row still says the cron reserves an addition of `order` without the purchases condition; `pr-w1d` rewrites the `autoscale_enabled` text in `platform/nodes.ts` too, and whichever branch merges second must keep the `purchases_enabled` condition |
| Credentials revision follows the route keyring and the shell: migration `0083`, on branch `pr-w2a` (2026-10-22; W2-A, S3-07; built and tested, not deployed) | **Before.** Only a change of the shell's state raised `credentials_revision` (`shellCredentialsRevision` in `node-shell.ts`), so a changed route keyring reached a running gateway only at the node's next start, and a keyring rotation could not be applied to a running node. **Built.** `credentialsRevision` in `node-credentials.ts` replaces `shellCredentialsRevision`. D1 holds a digest of the keyring the node was last handed, next to `shell_state`: `nodes.route_keyring_state` (SHA-256 of the keyring derived for the node: its active key ID, its key IDs and its keys, in whatever order the variable lists them), never a key. NULL is no record: the first request records and raises nothing, so a new node starts at revision 1. The desired page derives the keyring from `ROUTE_MASTER_KEYS` (no Cloudflare call) and compares it and the shell's state; the credentials read compares the same two. One statement writes the states and raises the revision once, whichever of them changed, and the page and the read name the same revision whichever of them sees a change first. The agent already reads its credentials again when the page's revision is above the one it applied; the page gains no order, so no database stops. A route keyring the Worker cannot read leaves the revision as it is and does not refuse the page, which carries the fence and the wakes: every page logs `node_keyring_unreadable` until the variable is fixed, and the credentials read fails as before. **What it does not do.** (1) A Tunnel token that changes at Cloudflare is not part of the revision, and no node reads sooner for it: a node learns of the token only from `GET /node/v1/credentials`, which hands out the current token with every read, and the agent restarts the Tunnel for a token that differs from the one it runs on (`gateway_secrets` in `service.rs`); a revision for the token would only renumber a response the node acts on anyway. A changed token therefore reaches a node at its next credentials read, which is the agent's start or a revision that rose for another reason; pushing it would need a periodic probe of every node's Tunnel, which is not built because no token change has been observed. (2) A keyring change restarts the Tunnel as well as the gateway. When the digest of the Tunnel token and the keyring that the agent keeps differs (making another key active is a change too, because the digest includes `active`), `apply_gateway_credentials` (`machine/node.rs`) orders a systemd Restart job for `pgcf-gateway.service` and for `pgcf-cloudflared.service` (`start_service` with `restart`, `units/mod.rs`), on every node at its next full pull (every 60 s, `apps/node-agent/README.md`) or at the pull of a wake. So each step of the rotation in `credentials.md` that changes the keyring (the new key beside the old, the new key active, the old key retired) restarts both on every node once. The gateway's socket handover covers only the gateway and ends its open client sessions; while `cloudflared` registers again, the Edge cannot reach the node at all and a new connection fails; that gap has not been measured. **Merge note.** Branch `pr-w2f` (unmerged) also adds `0083_single_archive_bucket.sql`, and no CI check enforces unique migration numbers; whichever of the two branches merges second renumbers its migration to `0084`, regenerates the Mermaider diagrams (`d1-core.md`, the manifest, `index.html`) and corrects the migration number in its plan row. (`pr-w2a` merged first; `pr-w2f` renumbered its migration to `0084` on 2026-10-22.) **Red then green:** `node-desired.test.ts` (the revision rises once for a key added beside the old one, for another active key, for a retired key and for a key replaced under its own ID, and not for the same keys in another order; the page orders nothing and the database is still running; D1 holds a digest and not the key; an unreadable keyring leaves the revision, the page answers and logs; a row that moved since it was read, for the keyring) and `node-credentials.test.ts` (a changed Tunnel token is handed out at the revision the node had and raises nothing; a changed keyring raises once; the page and the read agree whichever sees the change first). **Live acceptance still to do (S3-07):** apply `0083` with a fresh daily D1 export in place and deploy the Worker; read a node's row (the digest recorded, revision unchanged by the first record); run one real route-keyring rotation on EU1 with no database stopped (the new key beside the old with the old active: the node's next sample carries the new revision, and the gateway and `cloudflared` of the node restarted once; then the new key active, a fresh connection to a database on every node, and the old key retired) and record, per node and per step, the revision, the restarts of both units and the gap between the `cloudflared` restart and the Tunnel's connection being registered again (the time a new connection through the Edge fails). `credentials.md` describes it (DOC-2, pass 1, round 4). |
| Idmapped handoff of a database's mounts to a pooled slot, built on branch `cold-pd` (2026-10-20; the pool's package P-d), not deployed, called by the pool of P-e (`System::mount`) | **Built.** `units/idmap.rs`: a user namespace that maps the database's uid to the slot's uid, its gid to the slot's gid and the gateway's group to itself; for each mount `open_tree(OPEN_TREE_CLONE)` of the agent's mount, a check of the device, and `mount_setattr` with the idmap, nosuid, nodev and noexec (and noatime on a volume); a thread of its own that does `unshare(CLONE_FS)`, `setns` through the slot's pidfd and `move_mount` onto the same path, following no symlink at the end of it; no namespace descriptor is kept. Every clone is made `MS_PRIVATE` in the same `mount_setattr`, so it leaves the peer group of the agent's mount. Unit tests that run everywhere (the map lines, the attribute flags and the propagation of a clone, the struct size, the id and path checks) were written first and failed first. **Lab** (`units/idmap_lab.rs`, privileged, built only with `--cfg pgcf_idmap_lab`, not in CI), run inside `systemd-run --wait --pipe -p PrivateMounts=yes`, the mount namespace and propagation of `pgcf-agent.service` (every mount shared; the lab refuses a namespace with private mounts), on a laptop in a Debian 13 container with systemd 257 as PID 1 (Linux 6.8, aarch64; not EU1): the volume arrives at `/var/lib/pgcf/db/<id>` in a transient unit with `ProtectSystem=strict` and the other namespace directives of `pgcf-pg@.service`, and the rest of the file system stays read-only; the slot's user owns the volume and what it creates there is the database's on disk; the mounts show nosuid, nodev, noexec, idmapped (and noatime on the volume); PID 1 sees none of them; the slot's mount holds the filesystem until the slot ends, even after the agent unmounted its own, and a failed handoff holds nothing; the gateway's group dials a socket made in the idmapped tmpfs directory and sees the slot's uid and the listener's pid; a wrong device is refused and a symlink at the target is not followed; the slots' mounts are in peer groups of their own, a mount made on or under the agent's volume reaches neither of two slots, and a mount made under a slot's volume reaches neither the agent nor the other slot; eight threads handing over to eight slots at once, ten rounds, 30 repeated runs in that namespace, no failure. **Times** (the laptop's Docker VM, shared with other work, so the spread is the VM's; 24 handoffs of the volume and the socket directory, each into a slot of its own, in 11 runs of the debug build in the agent's namespace): p50 0.41 to 0.59 ms and p95 0.61 to 1.96 ms, the quietest run 0.41 / 0.61 ms. The user namespace alone took a p50 of 0.06 to 0.38 ms in a process of 16 MiB and 0.10 to 0.36 ms in one of 528 MiB (30 each, p95 0.14 to 3.2 ms), where a `fork` and its wait took a p50 of 0.32 to 1.04 ms at 16 MiB and 7.7 to 18.6 ms at 528 MiB: the child is made with `CLONE_VM`, so the time does not grow with the agent's memory. **Findings.** (1) The kernel refuses every write to an inode whose owner or group the mount cannot map (`EACCES`): the socket directory of the group `pgcf-gateway` could not hold PostgreSQL's socket until that group was mapped to itself, and a file in a volume that the database's uid and gid do not own is readable by the slot and not writable, even with mode 0666. P-e passes the gateway's gid, and the agent leaves nothing in a volume that PostgreSQL writes under another owner. (2) The first holder of the user namespace waited for the end of a pipe and deadlocked when two handoffs ran at once (each child had a copy of the other's write end); the child is now killed by signal and ends with the agent's thread if the agent dies. (3) `open_tree(OPEN_TREE_CLONE)` leaves the clone in the peer group of the agent's mount, and under `PrivateMounts=yes` every mount of the agent is shared: the slot's volume was a peer of the agent's, so a mount made on or under either appeared in the other and in every other holder of the volume, and the second round of the storm test stacked a clone that came back into the agent's namespace, so the next `open_tree` cloned a mount that was already idmapped and `mount_setattr` failed with `EPERM`. The first lab ran under `unshare --mount --propagation slave`, where the agent's mounts are private, and did not show it; it now runs in the agent's own propagation and the clone is `MS_PRIVATE`. |

| Slot supervisor `pgcf-archive slot <n>` on branch `cold-pa` (2026-10-20; package P-a of the cold 750 ms work), not deployed | **What.** A second mode of the signed `pgcf-archive` binary, standard library only, so the signed set of files does not change (`apps/pgcf-archive/src/slot.rs`, a dispatch in `main.rs`, Linux only). It binds `$RUNTIME_DIRECTORY/control`, reports `READY=1` and serves one line per connection, only to a peer whose `SO_PEERCRED` uid is 0 (any other peer is closed unheard). `ping` is answered `pgcf-slot/1 idle`. `exec <database> <major>` opens `/var/lib/pgcf/db/<id>/data` with `O_DIRECTORY` and `O_NOFOLLOW` (its owner must be the supervisor's own uid, the proof of the agent's idmapped mount), stats `/run/pgcf/<id>` (a directory of the same owner), takes an exclusive non-blocking `flock` on the data directory without close-on-exec, answers `exec <CLOCK_MONOTONIC microseconds>` and then execs exactly the `ExecStart=` of `pgcf-pg@.service`. Every refusal (`order`, `id`, `major`, `unbound`, `held`, `lock`) is answered and ends the supervisor with status 1; it never forks or mounts, and it takes no second order (the first `exec` replaces or ends it). The supervisor execs only on that order, and the agent has to send it only after it set the slot's limits, because an idle slot's memory limit (32 MiB in the design) is below `shared_buffers`. **Why the lock is mandatory (checked in the PostgreSQL sources).** `miscinit.c` reads `kill(pid, 0)` failing with `EPERM` as a stale `postmaster.pid`, and `sysv_shmem.c` reads `EACCES` on the old shared memory segment as a foreign segment (`SHMSTATE_FOREIGN`, counted as not in use), so PostgreSQL's own interlock fails between two uids even without `PrivateIPC`. A `flock` belongs to the open file description that PostgreSQL and every backend inherit, so it lasts until the last process of the slot has ended, orphaned backends included. It is per inode: the agent still has to try-lock the directory before every bind and keep its binding rule across volume generations. **Tests, written first.** Ten tests against a skeleton: 9 failed, the tenth is the entry point of the test processes. They run the supervisor as a real process (the test program starts itself again, because a process that execs cannot run inside a test) with a real `NOTIFY_SOCKET` datagram socket: the order table (ids, majors, junk), the configuration from the slot number and systemd, the argv equal to the `ExecStart=` parsed from the unit file, a peer that is not the agent, each refusal with its answer and exit status 1 and nothing run (an id that is no ID, a major, a directory owned by another uid, missing, a link, a file, no socket directory), the answer's clock between two readings of `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, a second supervisor on a held directory (`refused held`), the lock surviving the process that took it while a background child of the target holds it, a second order on a queued connection never acted on, and a real PostgreSQL 18 as the exec target (`postmaster.pid` names the supervisor's own PID, `select 1` answers, a second supervisor is refused, `pg_ctl stop` ends the process with status 0 and the lock is free). An eleventh test (the open flags) was added after the code. Seven broken variants each fail at least one test: no lock (3 tests), close-on-exec left set (3), no `O_NOFOLLOW` (2), no `O_DIRECTORY` (1), no peer check (1), no owner check (1), `stat` in place of `lstat` for the socket directory (1). **Measured.** 11 tests green in 0.8 to 1.2 s, ten runs in a row, in the pinned Rust 1.99.0 builder image (Alpine, AArch64) as a non-root user with `CI=1`, `--cpus 2` and PostgreSQL 18; `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and the whole crate's tests green. The x86-64 values of `O_DIRECTORY` (0x10000) and `O_NOFOLLOW` (0x20000) were checked against the source of libc 0.2.190; CI is the first x86-64 run. **Left for the live acceptance (the privileged lab of package P-e, then the live pool acceptance).** (1) The lab test of the judge's finding, which needs two uids: a second postmaster of another uid on the same data directory runs without the lock and is refused with it. (2) `flock`, `fcntl`, `getsockopt`, `accept4`, `clock_gettime` and `execve` under the slot unit's `SystemCallFilter` and `MemoryDenyWriteExecute`. (3) The root agent reaching `control` in the slot's own `RuntimeDirectory`, and `SO_PEERCRED` across the slot's namespaces. (4) The time from the order to the exec on EU1 (lab: 1.5 / 6.7 ms). (5) `Type=notify` with the supervisor's `READY=1` followed by PostgreSQL's own. Nothing starts the mode yet: the slot unit and the agent's side are other packages. |
