| Background jobs yield to cold requests, on branch `pr-bg` (2026-10-22) | **Disk.** The data disk's scheduler is `none`, so the `IOWeight=` of `pgcfbackup.slice` divides nothing. Built: `IOReadBandwidthMax=` and `IOWriteBandwidthMax=` of 32 MB/s each on `/dev/disk/by-partlabel/pgcf-lvm` in `pgcfbackup.slice` (a change of an existing host file, applied by `daemon_reload`; `host-files.ts` needs no new row). **Why not the others.** (1) `IODeviceLatencyTargetSec=` (io.latency) cannot work: Debian's kernel config says `# CONFIG_BLK_CGROUP_IOLATENCY is not set` (read in the package sources of 6.12.38-1 and 6.12.107-1, not of the image's 6.12.113), and the lab kernel, which lacks it too, had no `io.latency` file. (2) io.cost is built (`=y`) but off by default: it is switched on by a write to the root cgroup's `io.cost.qos` with the device's MAJ:MIN, which no unit can do, and it needs a cost model and QoS values per device. systemd's iocost udev rule applies solutions only for models in the benchmark database, which a virtual disk is not in; the kernel then picks its automatic model, and for a disk that reports `rotational=1` (the lab VM's disks did) that is the hard-disk model of 370 random IOPS (`ioc_autop_idx`, 6.12), which would throttle the databases too. (3) A scheduler: BFQ is a module (`=m`), mq-deadline has no cgroup weights, both change the path of every database's I/O, and a udev rule is outside `HOST_FILE_DIRECTORIES` (a contract and agent change, or a new image). The caps touch only the jobs' bytes, need no scheduler or calibration, and are the mechanism the agent already uses per database (`io.max`). They are not work-conserving: a restore writes at most 32 MB/s. **How the rule finds the disk.** By the label `pgcf-lvm` of the LVM partition that the first boot makes (`repart.d/30-lvm.conf`) and that the agent builds the volume group on; systemd follows the link and takes the partition's whole disk, which also holds the root filesystem where barman spools. No device number is in the image, and a test ties the path to the label. **Values.** 32 MB/s is 3.8 times the 8.5 MB/s the lab's base backup moved (557 MB in 65 s) and 30 % of the 106 MB/s that EU1's disk reads at random (cold-path disk lab, sda, scheduler `none`: 13,555 IOPS of 8 KiB at queue depth 32; sequential 1 MiB about 1 GB/s); one big job runs at a time (`BIG_JOBS` 1). **Lab** (privileged Debian 13 container, systemd 257.13, a 6.8 kernel): the slice passes `systemd-analyze verify`; with the link `io.max` read `253:0 rbps=32000000 wbps=32000000` (the link led to a partition, `vda1`); a reload alone left the running slice's old value, though `systemctl show` reported the new one, and the next unit started in the slice applied it; `set-property --runtime` applied at once; without the link the job started uncapped (systemd's source logs a warning and skips). A release therefore reaches the slice with the next backup job. **Revert.** systemd writes `io.max` only for the devices that a unit lists, so a release that deletes the two lines does not lift the cap (verified twice in systemd 257.13 labs, the second of this round: after the deletion a reload and the next job in the slice left `253:0 rbps=32000000 wbps=32000000`, an empty runtime value left it too, and only the explicit `infinity` below or a reboot cleared it). What lifts it: a release that keeps both lines with `infinity` as the size on the same device (a reload alone left the cap, the next job in the slice wrote an empty `io.max`), or at once on one node `systemctl set-property --runtime pgcfbackup.slice "IOReadBandwidthMax=/dev/disk/by-partlabel/pgcf-lvm infinity" "IOWriteBandwidthMax=/dev/disk/by-partlabel/pgcf-lvm infinity"` (`io.max` empty; the same command with `32M` set the cap again). An empty runtime value lifted the cap only while the lines were still in the unit file. **A runtime change outlives the releases (finding of the third verification, lab repeated).** `set-property --runtime` writes `50-IOReadBandwidthMax.conf` and `50-IOWriteBandwidthMax.conf` to `/run/systemd/system.control/pgcfbackup.slice.d/`, which override the unit file and every later release of it until the node reboots. Lab (privileged Debian 13 container, systemd 257.13-1~deb13u1, a 6.8.0 kernel, `/dev/disk/by-partlabel/pgcf-lvm` linked to the VM's disk): after `infinity` and then `32M` at runtime, a file with `48M`, a reload and the next job in the slice left `io.max` at `rbps=32000000 wbps=32000000`; after `systemctl revert pgcfbackup.slice` the next job wrote `rbps=48000000 wbps=48000000`. A file with `infinity` over a runtime `32M` drop-in left the cap too, and the revert followed by the next job emptied `io.max`; a revert after `infinity` alone returned the shipped value at the next job. So the one-node `infinity` command and any other runtime size (the A/B of the Open row) end with `systemctl revert pgcfbackup.slice`, and the next job in the slice applies the file; the lasting way to lift the cap is the release with `infinity`. The slice's comment and the agent's README say the same. **Agent.** `backup_if_due` is the one place that decides a base backup is due; an idle sleep and the daily pass of an always-warm database both ask it. It now asks `backup_waits` too: a due backup is put off while a start is queued or in flight on the node (`starting + queued` of the admission loop) and in the first 60 s after any database on the node became ready (`Core::newest_ready_ms`: the newest `awake_since_ms` over the node's databases, set by a wake, a build and the adoption of a unit that runs). It is put off for at most 10 minutes from the first time in an awake session (`BACKUP_PUT_OFF_MAX_MS`, the wait after a failed backup; a sleep forgets the clock, so a session never inherits the wait of an earlier one), then it is taken whatever the node does. **Bound (corrected after the verifications of rounds 2 and 3).** The first build let a put-off idle sleep go on without the backup; then nothing asks for it again before the next idle sleep, which comes after the next wake, and a database is never woken for a backup, so for a database that sleeps the wall-clock wait had no bound (days), and the WAL a restore replays would have grown by the whole next awake session. Now a put-off idle sleep does not put the database to sleep (`Slept::BackupPutOff`): it stays Ready and the next idle pass (`idle_poll`, 5 s) asks again. **What that bounds.** For a database that stays up the backup is taken within 10 minutes and one idle pass of the first put-off, whatever the node does, in both of its uses. Idle: at its idle sleep. Used meanwhile (a client comes back inside the window; a busy database is never idle, so no idle sleep comes, and the wait would have lasted the whole busy session, which has no bound): once the put-off has lasted 10 minutes the idle pass asks `spawn_served_backup`, which takes the backup while the database serves, as it does daily for an always-warm database (`sleep_after_seconds` null; now also a database that was put off for the longest). **What it does not bound.** An early sleep. A wake that waits for room (a queued start, which is also what puts the backup off) orders the early sleep of the idle database unused longest, typically the one that was put off; an early sleep takes no backup (as before this change) and clears the clock (`backup_put_off_ms`), so the backup is taken at the idle sleep after the database's next wake, which may be days away, and the WAL a restore replays then includes that whole next session, not 10 minutes of it. A backup in front of the early sleep would delay the wake that waits for room, which is why it takes none; the put-off makes the case likelier because the database stays awake longer. `a_database_that_sleeps_without_its_backup_waits_anew_at_its_next_wake` covers the early sleep itself (backup unchanged, the next session waits anew); the Rig never carries out the early-sleep orders of admission, so `a_wake_that_waits_for_room_puts_off_the_backup_of_an_idle_database_too` asserts Ready only because nothing reclaims the database there. Also as before this change: a database that is used without a pause longer than its idle time and was never put off takes no backup until its idle sleep. WAL archiving goes on in all of these cases, so the RPO does not change; only the age of the newest base backup, and the WAL a restore replays, grow. `backup_put_off` is logged once per session with the wakes on the node and the age of the newest database to become ready (`age_of_newest_ready_ms`). **The first minute is node-wide (round 3, finding 1).** The first build counted the minute from the backup's own database. The contract's idle time is at least 60 s (`packages/contracts/src/node-link.ts`) and the idle check counts from `awake_since_ms`, so the backup of an idle sleep is never inside its own database's first minute and the rule did nothing on that path; the statements after the WAKE of database A, whose start was over (`starting` and `queued` 0), met the backup of database B at B's next idle pass. Now `backup_waits` is given the newest `awake_since_ms` of the node. A stream of cold requests less than 60 s apart keeps every backup off until its own 10-minute cap, and the backups then start under that load: the cap is the bound, not the quiet. **Tests, red first.** `infra/node-image/background-io.test.ts` (new file) failed on `IOReadBandwidthMax is set once` (0 !== 1) before the slice was changed; its other two tests (the databases' slice has no cap, no unit asks for io.latency) guard and were green from the start. In the agent, the unit test of `backup_waits` and two tests on real PostgreSQL 18 (`idle_pass` and `sleep` with a real admission permit as the wake on the node) failed against a rule that never waits (`assertion failed: backup_waits(Some(now - 59_999), 0, None, now)`, the idle sleep took the backup under a running wake, `timed out: the backup put off`) and passed with it. **Round 2 (findings of the independent verification).** The test of the first build for a put-off idle sleep (it expected the sleep to go on) is replaced by four on real PostgreSQL 18 through `idle_pass` with a real admission permit or a real queued request (no room): `an_idle_database_stays_awake_while_a_wake_runs_and_its_backup_is_taken_at_the_next_pass_after_it` (the database stays Ready and running, a second pass keeps the first put-off timestamp, the pass after the wake takes the backup and sleeps), `a_wake_that_waits_for_room_puts_off_the_backup_of_an_idle_database_too` (a queued wake with none in flight), `an_idle_sleep_takes_the_backup_whatever_the_node_does_once_it_was_put_off_the_longest` (30 s short of the cap: put off; at the cap: taken under a running wake) and `a_database_that_sleeps_without_its_backup_waits_anew_at_its_next_wake`. They failed against the first build (three with `left: Asleep, right: Ready`, the fourth with `left: NotRunning, right: Proven` because the idle sleep had already slept) and pass. Mutation checks on the green code, run in the pinned builder image as a non-root user with CI=1 and `--cpus 2`, each caught by the named test and no other: `awake.starting + awake.queued` to `awake.starting` fails the queued-wake test only (the call site counted queued wakes in no test before); `if put_off.is_none()` to `if true` fails the first test only (the put-off timestamp moved by 65 ms; before, all 24 backup tests passed it); removing the reset of the clock at a sleep fails the fourth only; `backup_waits` that never waits fails 6 of 7; the first build's sleep that goes on fails 4; not resetting the clock after a taken backup fails the daily-backup test. Two existing tests now put their database up for a minute first, as the rule says (without it `an_idle_sleep_takes_the_base_backup_that_is_due_before_it_stops_the_database` fails: the backup is put off); the burst test sets the same edge, because the contract's longest burst is 60 s. **Round 3 tests, red first.** `the_backup_of_an_idle_database_waits_for_the_first_minute_after_a_wake_of_another` (real PostgreSQL 18: A woken by `wake` just now and Ready with no start queued or in flight, B idle with a due backup; B is put off and stays Ready, and once A's minute is over the next pass takes B's backup and puts it to sleep) and `a_database_that_is_used_takes_the_backup_it_was_put_off_for_while_it_serves_once_the_wait_is_over` (B busy after a put-off, with a wake in flight: 30 s short of the cap nothing is taken, at the cap the backup is taken while B stays Ready and in use). Mutation checks on the green code in the pinned builder image, as a non-root user with CI=1 and `--cpus 2`, each caught by the named test and no other of the 29 backup tests: the first build's rule (`backup_waits` given the backup's own database's `awake_since_ms`) fails the first (`left: Asleep, right: Ready`: B's backup started under A's first minute), and the idle pass without the put-off clause fails the second (`timed out: the backup of a database that is used`). The first test brings B up after A because the Rig runs every database as one user and the agent's archive table names a database by its user: with B first, B's WAL was archived as A's and B's sleep proof ended in `archive_timeout`. Gates of the round: `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy -p pgcf-node-agent --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` and `cargo test -p pgcf-node-agent --locked` (597 passed, 21 ignored) in the pinned builder image; the two new tests five more times alone, 5 of 5 green. Not deployed, nothing measured live; the A/B is in the Open row. |
| A start that fails after its unit is up is proven asleep, on branch `pr-fs` (2026-10-22; replaces the hypothesis of a resume that arrives during a slow sleep proof) | **Observed** (EU1, 2026-10-20 01:28 UTC, live finding of the 1,000-cycle run: 2 of 1,002 resumes failed, all 1,002 suspends succeeded). A resume at generation 201 answered `release_failed` while its PostgreSQL ran for 83 s: it started at 01:28:04.236, was ready at 04.565 and kept running until 01:29:28.6. The suspend that followed succeeded in 0.75 s from the stale proven-sleep record of the earlier sleep, so it stopped nothing. The next resume (01:29:27) was refused `unproven` by the `pg_control` check, and the checkpoint at 01:29:27.43 was the agent's recovery proof. The `node_wake` line of the first resume has the steps admission, volume_check, repair_check, pg_control, config and archive and no start step (total 1,000 ms), so the machine's start returned an error after the unit was up. The agent's journal of those minutes was gone (NEW-01) and the code dropped the error, so the class of the error is not known. **Not a race with a slow sleep.** The sleep before the first resume took 5.2 s, but the resume was created 0.48 s after it ended; the suspends of the run have median 3.29 s, p95 4.93 s, p99 7.57 s and max 24.65 s, and many slower sleeps were followed by resumes that succeeded. **Cause in the code.** (1) `start_unit` dropped the machine's error (the `map_err(\|_\| StartFailure::Failed)` and the `Ok(Err(_))` branch) and wrote no event. (2) `after_failed_start` read the unit with `unit_awake(db, false)`: a unit whose state could not be read counted as asleep, and the phase went `Asleep` with PostgreSQL running (the live case), while the start's permit kept counting its memory; a unit read as awake left the phase `Starting` and the function returned. **Change** (`apps/node-agent/src/agent/power.rs` and the test machine; no contract, vector or migration). Every `StartFailure::Failed` (three places make it) writes one event `unit_start_failed` with the database, the kind of the start (`wake`, `create`, `recovery`, `move`, `restore`) and the class of the error from `error_code` (`bus_<name>`, the bus's own error name such as `bus_limits_exceeded` or `bus_no_reply`, for an error reply of the bus or of systemd to a method call or to a property read; `units_bus` for a bus error with no name of its own: a connection that broke, an I/O failure or a reply the agent could not read; `units_unexpected`; `job_<result>`; `not_ready_<reason>`; `admission_stopped`), never the error's text. `units_code` (`diagnostics.rs`) named only a method call's error reply (`zbus::Error::MethodError`, from `StartUnit`, `GetUnit`) by the bus's error name; an error reply to a property read (`Properties.Get`) whose name is one of `fdo::Error`'s (`LimitsExceeded`, `NoReply`, `AccessDenied`, `Failed` and the like) comes back from zbus 5.19.0 as `zbus::Error::FDO`, and every one of those was `units_bus`, whether the bus refused or gave no reply. It now names an `FDO` error by the bus's error name as well, so `units_bus` is left for an error with no name. `after_failed_start` reads the unit with `unknown = true`, as `late_failure` always did (and `late_failure` is now this function): a unit that is awake or cannot be read is stopped without a proof (`stop_unproven`), the phase is `Unproven`, and recovery (7.10) starts the database through admission, lets it archive and proves the sleep before any wake; only a unit read as stopped leaves the database `Asleep`. A refused admission, whose unit was never asked to start, goes straight back to `Asleep` without a read of the unit. The wake still answers `release_failed`: the change makes the failure safe and visible, it does not hide it. **Tests, red then green** on real PostgreSQL 18.6 (`power.rs`; the test machine's new `Local::fail_next_start_after_up` ends `start` with the bus's `LimitsExceeded` error reply, a `MethodError` as `Units::state`'s `GetUnit` gets it past dbus-daemon's limit of pending replies, once the unit is active; `bus_refused()` built a `Failure` that no real call returns): `a_start_that_fails_after_its_unit_is_up_and_is_read_awake_is_proven_asleep` and `a_start_that_fails_after_its_unit_is_up_and_cannot_be_read_is_proven_asleep` (the second with `set_units_unreadable`). Red against the old code: the wake line was the live one (`release_failed`, no start step); the first test found the phase still `Starting` after the wake answered, the second timed out after 10 s waiting for the unit to stop and its sleep to be proven (the postmaster kept running). Green: the phase is `Unproven`, recovery starts the database (the `admission` event `start: recovery`), the unit stops and the sleep is proven (`Asleep`, not running), the admission's awake set is empty, one `unit_start_failed` line carries the kind `wake` and the class `bus_limits_exceeded`, and the next wake starts the database and finds its 3,000 rows. The class test of `diagnostics.rs` (`storage_and_unit_failures_are_named_by_what_failed_never_by_their_text`) was extended first and failed against `units_code` (`units_bus` for an `FDO` `LimitsExceeded`, where `bus_limits_exceeded` was wanted); it now also holds `bus_no_reply` for an `FDO` `NoReply` and `units_bus` for an I/O error and for a `Failure`, and none of the reply's words reaches the class. |

| Node loss deletes the node's DNS records, on branch `pr-w2b` (package W2-B, 2026-10-22), not deployed | **Found** (S0-03, 2026-10-22): a stale proxied CNAME of a retired node was still in the gateway zone and was removed by hand. **Cause in the code.** `ensureNodeTunnel` makes `pgcf-node-<id>` (and, while `NODE_SHELL_HOSTNAME` is `true`, `pgcf-shell-<id>`) as proxied CNAMEs of the node's Tunnel, but the fence's `deleteTunnel` deleted only the Tunnel by name, so a lost node's records stayed pointing at a deleted Tunnel for good. **Built.** After the Tunnel, `deleteTunnel` looks up the three hostnames a node has or had (`nodeHostnames`: the gateway's, the shell's and the shell's former `-ssh` name, one function that credentials and fencing share) in the zone `NODE_GATEWAY_ZONE_ID` and deletes a CNAME only if its target is `<id>.cfargotunnel.com` of a Tunnel listed under the node's name, deleted ones included. A record with the node's name that points elsewhere, and every other record of the zone, is not touched. The Tunnel goes first, because it is what fences the node; the records follow in the same step, so a step that failed on them is repeated whole (the listing still names the deleted Tunnel and its identifier finds the records), and a repeat of a finished step changes nothing. The Tunnel is deleted whatever the zone is (round 2, finding of the independent verification: the first build checked the zone before it listed the Tunnel, so a node with a Tunnel that was lost while `NODE_GATEWAY_ZONE_ID` or `NODE_GATEWAY_DOMAIN` was missing or unusable kept its Tunnel, the network fence, alive and was never ordered off, where before this package the token and the account alone fenced it). Only after the Tunnel loop, a node that has a Tunnel under its name (found, deleted ones included) and no usable zone fails the step as `fence_unconfigured`; the step is retried whole until the zone is there, like any other failure of the records, and meanwhile the node's Tunnel is gone and its instance is not yet ordered off (the cron stops a node at its first failing step). A Tunnel that is not found is `tunnel_unknown` before the zone is looked at. **Open for the Workers VPC change (critic item 19):** a deploy that retires the public gateway hostnames and removes the zone variables would hold every later fence at `fence_unconfigured` after its Tunnel, so that change deletes this records step together with the variables. No new fence step, no column and no migration: `tunnel_deleted_at` is set once Tunnel and records are gone. **Token.** The API Worker uses one secret, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, for the Tunnel and the records (`node-credentials.ts` makes them, `fence-actions.ts` deletes them); it needs Account: Cloudflare Tunnel: Edit and Zone: DNS: Edit on the gateway zone only. The operator installation, credentials and recovery runbooks and the example config say so; the token's real permissions are a private Worker secret and were not read. **Tests, red then green** (`fence-actions.test.ts`, on the stateful Cloudflare double of `node-tunnel.test.ts`, which now also deletes Tunnels and lists deleted ones as the API does). Round 2, red first, three tests: a node with a Tunnel and no or an unusable zone has its Tunnel deleted, no record touched, fails `fence_unconfigured`, and the repeat with the zone deletes the records; a Tunnel that is not found is `tunnel_unknown` with no zone; the Worker's variables test sees the Tunnel deleted before the failure (the first build's tests pinned zero calls). Green after the change, with a guard that never failed: a record that has the node's name but points at another Tunnel, or is an A record, is left. Also tested: the repeat changes nothing, a node that never made a Tunnel needs no zone, and the zone is taken from the Worker's variables. **Not measured live.** See the open row of this package. |

| Role names of the Kubernetes runtime released: migration `0085`, on branch `pr-w2c` (2026-10-22; W2-C, S2-04; built and tested, not deployed) | **Before.** The contract, the API, the Edge, the gateway and the node refused `streaming_replica` and every name that starts with `cnpg_` (CloudNativePG's roles), and the API refused to create or delete `pgcf_maintenance`, a role no code of the node runtime creates. **Built.** What a customer role cannot take is four exact names and a prefix. `postgres` is the node's superuser and `pgcf_backup` is the node's backup role (below): both are the node's own, not PostgreSQL's. `public` and `none` are the two exact names PostgreSQL itself refuses in `CREATE ROLE` (below). The `pg_` prefix is PostgreSQL's reservation for its predefined roles (`RESERVED_ROLE_NAMES` and `RESERVED_ROLE_PREFIXES` in `ids-core.ts`, read by `RoleName`, by the Edge's `isRoleName`, by the gateway's `valid_role` through `protocol.generated.json`, and by the node's page rules through `node.generated.json`). `MAINTENANCE_ROLE` and `maintenance.ts` are deleted with its uses: the `RoleCreate` name and `member_of` refinements, the `refineRoles` rule of the desired page, `deleteRole` (a role of that name is now unknown, `404`), and `roles_valid` in `node_link.rs`. The OpenAPI texts and `integrator-handover.md` say the same. **The D1 column was the second place.** `roles.name` carried the same two names in a `CHECK` (`0001`), which this package's file list did not name: with the contract alone, `POST /v1/databases/{id}/roles` with `cnpg_app` would pass the zod schema and fail at the insert, on the `CHECK`. Migration `0085` builds the table again, because SQLite cannot change a `CHECK` in place: the same columns in the same order, the `CHECK` of `name` without the two terms and with `pgcf_backup`, `public` and `none` added (`postgres`, `pg_*` and the identifier rule stay), the primary key and `roles_one_owner_idx`, and every row copied unchanged, tombstones included; a row named `pgcf_backup`, `public` or `none` fails that `CHECK`, the migration stops and the table stays as it was. Nothing references `roles`, so no foreign key is in play. It is numbered `0085`, the next free number after `0084_single_archive_bucket` of W2-F (11.1). **Merge note.** The migration was `0084` until `pr-w2f` (one archive bucket for every region) merged first with `0084_single_archive_bucket.sql`, which is applied on Dev (the Done row "G8 one archive bucket: the cutover on Dev, steps 1 to 11"). No CI check enforces unique migration numbers, so the merge of `origin/main` `f5d699c6` into this branch renumbered the file to `0085`, regenerated the Mermaider diagrams (`d1-core.md`, the manifest, `index.html`), and corrected the number in this row, the Open row, the decisions in 11.5, the migration's header and `role-names-migration.test.ts`, whose seed insert of `regions` also lost the two columns that `0084` dropped. **Deploy order: the check and the migration first, then the node release, the API Worker and the Edge Worker; until the API Worker of this change is out, the freeze holds back every other change of main, Worker and migration alike, and not `0085`.** Why the order is hard. (a) `0085` goes first because it is the part that closes names, and the old Workers are safe under it. The three narrowed names (`pgcf_backup`, `public`, `none`) are accepted today by the old API and by D1; from the first node on R-2, which refuses a page that names one (`roles_valid`), until `0085`, a role of such a name created through the old API would be refused by every full pull of that node. After `0085` D1 refuses them, and the old API's insert fails on the `CHECK`: the error is not a `UNIQUE` failure, so `isConstraintError` does not map it and the old Worker answers `500` where this change answers `400` (the fourth review took the validation out of the way in a scratch copy: `{"name":"public"}` gave `expected 500 to be 400`); it creates nothing. `0085` opens nothing: the old `RoleName` still refuses `cnpg_*` and `streaming_replica`, the old `RoleCreate` refinement and `deleteRole` still refuse `pgcf_maintenance`, a restore copies only names that D1 already holds (`restore.ts`), and the old Edge refuses all of them as well. (b) The API Worker of this change waits for R-2. The desired page carries the node's release as well as its databases (`link/desired.rs`, `Desired.release`). A node below R-2 (the node release that holds this change) refuses the whole page that names such a role (`desired_page_valid`; "Cloudflare desired page invalid"), tombstones included (a deleted role is listed in the page as an absent role of the same name, and `roles_valid` checks its name), and applies nothing of the page. What that costs: a full pull is refused every time, and so is each targeted pull (`?ids=`, sent by a change to or a wake of a database) that names the database; a targeted pull for another database of the node is a valid page and carries the release too (`pull_page` calls `consider_update`), so a newer release can still reach the node through one. After the start, a refused pull only logs `desired_pull_failed`. **At every start of the agent** (a release install, a reboot, a crash), `start` asks for the first full page and retries it without end (`first_page_failed`, backoff to 30 s), and the gateway is served only after that page: **the node accepts no new connection for any of its databases**, not only for the one with the role. Only deleting the role row in D1 (after every role that is a member of it has lost the name, as in step (0): a row deleted first leaves them a membership of an absent role, which the page refuses) or the operator shell's binary update frees it; a `DELETE` through the API does not, because it leaves a tombstone, which the page still carries until the node observes the removal (`node-observations.ts`), and a node that refuses the page never does. (c) The deployed Edge is the TypeScript `apps/edge`, which bundles the old list from `ids-core` (`isRoleName` in `apps/edge/src/index.ts` for a connection, `edge-sql.ts` for SQL over HTTP). Until it is redeployed, a role of such a name is created but every connection as it answers `28P01`. The steps. (0) **Check, as the last act before `0085`:** the query `SELECT database_id, name FROM roles WHERE name IN ('pgcf_backup','public','none') OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(member_of_json) WHERE value IN ('pgcf_backup','public','none'))` answers no row, so D1 holds no row of `roles` named `pgcf_backup`, `public` or `none` and no role that is a member of one, tombstones included. The second half is needed: the old API accepts a `member_of` that names any live role except the owner `app` and `pgcf_maintenance`, so `{"name":"x","member_of":["pgcf_backup"]}` is accepted while a `pgcf_backup` row is live, and only the API's `DELETE` looks for members (`role_has_members`), a hard delete in D1 does not. If the named row alone is deleted in D1, `x` keeps `member_of: ["pgcf_backup"]`, `refineRoles` refuses a membership of a role that is not present (the contract vector `NodeDesiredPage/member-of-an-absent-role` is false), `NodeDesiredPage.parse` (`node-desired.ts`) throws for the whole page, and the API answers `500` to every full pull of the node that holds the database. Step (2)'s install restarts that node's agent, which never gets past its first full page, so the node accepts no new connection for any of its databases: the cost of (b), caused by the row's own fix. After step (3) `DesiredRole.member_of` is `RoleName[]`, which refuses the three names, so the new API fails the same way on such a member. **A row found is handled in this order, in one D1 batch (one transaction): the members first, then the rows.** (i) `UPDATE roles SET member_of_json = (SELECT json_group_array(value) FROM json_each(member_of_json) WHERE value NOT IN ('pgcf_backup','public','none')) WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(member_of_json) WHERE value IN ('pgcf_backup','public','none'))` takes the three names out of the member lists, tombstones included (or a member is deleted through the API first; its tombstone keeps `member_of_json` and counts as a hit until the node has observed the removal); (ii) `DELETE FROM roles WHERE name IN ('pgcf_backup','public','none')` deletes the rows the names stand for, tombstones included, which only D1 can do. The row is never deleted first. A row that appears after the check makes the migration stop with the table as it was, and is handled in the same order. A hit on `pgcf_backup`, by name or by membership, also means that the node altered barman's role on that database (below: the `ALTER ROLE` with the customer's attributes, no `LOGIN` repair, the memberships in `pg_checkpoint` and `pg_monitor` revoked); deleting the rows does not repair it, so that database's base backups need repair, `LOGIN` and both memberships restored and a base backup taken, which no code of this package does. (1) **A fresh daily D1 export is in place, then `0085` is applied from the commit that merged this branch.** `0082` of the dead capacity row, `0083` of W2-A and `0084` of W2-F are applied already: the API Worker of main `f50f231c` is deployed and `0084` was applied after it (the Done rows "Release of main `69d2b245` live on EU1" for `0082` and `0083`, 2026-10-22 21:18 UTC, and "G8 one archive bucket: the cutover on Dev, steps 1 to 11" for `0084`, 2026-10-23 02:29 to 02:30 UTC), and main `c788749b` differs from `f50f231c` in the docs and in one API change that is not deployed: `f09d26fb` (owner decision O6, 11.3), which shortens the peak window of placement from 7 to 3 days (`PEAK_WINDOW_MS` in `apps/api/src/domain/placement.ts` and a comment in `apps/api/src/node-actor.ts`; API only, no migration and no node side). Its deploy is the precondition of this merge (the Freeze paragraph), and with it no migration other than `0085` is pending. `wrangler d1 migrations apply` applies every migration that is pending in the directory it runs from, and the directory of main's head may by then hold the migration of an API change that merged after this branch (the Freeze paragraph). So the apply runs from a checkout of the commit that merged this branch, whose directory ends at `0085`, and `wrangler d1 migrations list` from that checkout shows `0085` as the only pending migration just before the apply; if it lists any other, nothing is applied until the reason is known (`0082`, `0083` or `0084` missing in D1, or a file that does not belong to that commit). From main's head the apply is allowed only when `wrangler d1 migrations list` shows `0085` as the only pending migration there too. (2) **R-2, the signed release `sha-<first 12 digits of the merge commit>` of the Freeze paragraph, is registered, assigned and observed on every node of every region, and every image a node can be installed or recovered from holds R-2 or newer.** The image bakes in the four binaries (`infra/node-image/README.md`), so a node installed from an older image, such as the one the G9 recover drill builds, has the cost of (b) as soon as a database with such a role is placed on it. (3) **The API Worker of this change is deployed once R-2 has converged**, and not before: a Worker deployed earlier lets a role of a released name be created for nodes that refuse its page. It is deployed from main's head, so the Worker of an API change that merged during the freeze goes out with it, and that change's migration is applied after it (the Freeze paragraph). **Freeze.** R-2 is the signed release `sha-<first 12 digits of the merge commit>`, cut from the commit that merged this branch, so it carries this API change and no later one. **This branch's merge is pushed to main alone, and its `sign-release` job is green before anything else is pushed to main.** Only a push to main builds and signs a release: `sign-release` has `if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, the release id is `sha-` and the first 12 digits of `github.sha`, and the signer refuses a token of a dispatch (`docs/operations/release-signing.md`). GitHub runs CI for the head SHA of a push only, and merge trains push several merges at once (train 2 put `pr-w2a`, `pr-w2b`, `pr-w2d` and `pr-w2g` in one push). If a later branch were pushed with this merge, no signed build of the merge commit would exist, main cannot be rewound, and the operator would be left with the build of the head as R-2, which carries the later change's node side ahead of its API Worker, which the freeze holds back: the inversion this paragraph exists to prevent. The CI concurrency group of the pushes to main also keeps one pending run only (`cancel-in-progress` is false for a push, so a running run goes on), so a second push replaces the merge's run if that run is still waiting for an earlier one. The artifacts of the run (the release files and the signature) are kept for 7 days (`retention-days: 7`), so R-2 is registered within 7 days of the run, or the run is re-run, which builds and signs it again. From the merge of this branch until step (3), no API Worker is deployed from main and no migration of another API change is applied; step (3) is the first deploy from main, and `0085` is not held by the freeze: step (1) applies it. **Precondition, for every change and not only for the dead capacity row:** every API change on main at the moment this branch merges is deployed before the merge, or from the commit just before it. Otherwise R-2, which is cut from the merge commit, carries that change's node side, while the freeze holds its API Worker back until R-2 has converged: the node side would reach the nodes before the API Worker it depends on, which reverses an "API first" order. Example: `pr-w2f` is on main, and its API Worker and its migration `0084` are deployed before this branch merges. At the time of this text one API change is pending: `f09d26fb` (owner decision O6, 11.3; the peak window of placement is 3 days instead of 7: `PEAK_WINDOW_MS` in `apps/api/src/domain/placement.ts` and a comment in `apps/api/src/node-actor.ts`; API only, no migration, no node side). The Worker that carries `pr-w1c`, `pr-w1d` (with `0082`, the dead capacity row), `pr-w1e`, `pr-w2a` (`0083`) and `pr-w2f` (`0084`) is the deployed Worker of main `f50f231c`, and main `c788749b` differs from it in `f09d26fb` and in docs. **The deploy of the Worker of `f09d26fb` is the precondition of this merge**: it is deployed from main `c788749b`, or from the commit just before the merge of this branch, before this branch is pushed. Because it has no node side, R-2 would not carry anything of it ahead of its Worker; what the freeze would cost instead is that the 3-day window stays undeployed until step (3), and the runs that wait for it (the md class and the restore into a smaller class, 11.3) wait with it. If it is deployed first, this paragraph and step (1) record the deploy in its place (the time and the Worker version) and name nothing as pending. **A change that merges after this branch, during the freeze, waits until step (3), Worker and migration alike.** The precondition covers only what is on main at the moment this branch merges. A later change's migration is not applied with `0085`: step (1) applies from the checkout of the merge commit, and a `wrangler d1 migrations apply` from main's head would apply every pending file, among them one that drops what the deployed Worker reads (as `0084` of `pr-w2f` dropped the two `regions` archive columns that the Worker before it reads), before the Worker that no longer reads it is out. Such a Worker goes out with this change's API Worker in step (3), a deploy from main's head that carries both, and its migration is applied after that deploy, in the order of its own row; a later change with a migration that only adds is applied before its Worker, one that drops, after it. A node side of such a change stays out of R-2, which is cut from the merge commit, and reaches the nodes in a later release, after its Worker. Alternatively no API change merges into main between this merge and step (3), and nothing waits. (4) The Edge Worker is deployed once R-2 has converged. Deploying it earlier is harmless, because the old API still refuses these names. **Rollback.** Once a role of a released name exists, a rollback of a node below R-2 installs and starts the old agent, which is the start of (b): every database on that node refuses new connections until the role row is deleted in D1 or the operator shell's binary update installs R-2 or newer again. **A rollback of the API Worker below this change costs the same, and is node-wide too.** The old API builds the whole node page with `NodeDesiredPage.parse` (`apps/api/src/domain/node-desired.ts`), and in the old contract `DesiredRole.name` and `DesiredRoleRemoval.name` are `RoleName` (`packages/contracts/src/node-link.ts` of main `f5d699c6`), which refuses `cnpg_*` and `streaming_replica`; the old `refineRoles` refuses `pgcf_maintenance`. Once a role of a released name is in D1 (tombstones included), the old Worker answers `500` to every full pull of every node that holds that database, and to every targeted pull that names it, so that database can no longer wake or take a change. At the next start of the agent of such a node (a release install, a reboot or a crash) `start` retries the first full page without end (`first_page_failed`), and the node accepts no new connection for any of its databases: the cost of (b), per node and not per database. The old `NodeObservation` schema also refuses the `roles.removed` and `roles.blocked` entries that name such a role, so the node's report of a removal is refused as well. The API Worker is therefore not rolled back below this change while such a role exists, unless those role rows are deleted in D1 first, and the roles that are a member of them lose the name from their `member_of_json` before that, in the order of step (0): the old contract refuses a `member_of` that names `cnpg_*` or `streaming_replica`, and refuses a membership of a role that is absent, so a member left behind fails the whole page as the row did. Nothing reserved it, so any integrator key could create a customer role of that name. The node then applied it as `ALTER ROLE "pgcf_backup"` with the customer's `valid_until`, `connection_limit` and password, and the membership reconciliation (`roles.rs`) revoked `pg_checkpoint` and `pg_monitor` from barman's role. Deleting it did not repair that: the backup role holds five privileges PostgreSQL records as dependencies (`CONNECT` on database `postgres`, and `EXECUTE` on `pg_backup_start`, `pg_backup_stop`, `pg_switch_wal` and `pg_create_restore_point`; five `pg_shdepend` entries, checked on PostgreSQL 18), so `DROP ROLE` fails, `remove()` sets it `NOLOGIN` and reports `role_not_droppable`, and `ensure_backup_role` never restores `LOGIN` or the memberships. The base backups of that database stop for good. The exact name is therefore reserved in this package: `RESERVED_ROLE_NAMES`, the `CHECK` of `0085` and the vectors, and so the API, the Edge, the gateway and the node's page rules refuse it (decision `W2-C` in 11.5). This narrows the contract, the opposite direction to the three released names, so run **the check of step (0) as the last act before `0085`** (it answers no row: no role named `pgcf_backup`, `public` or `none` and no role that is a member of one, tombstones included): the copy of `0085` stops on a name, and a node on R-2 refuses the page of its database. `0085` goes before R-2 because it is what closes the names: the old API accepts them until it is applied, and after it the old API's insert fails on the `CHECK` and answers `500`, creating nothing. A row that appears after the check makes the migration stop with the table as it was; it is handled in the order of step (0). **Found in the third review, and fixed here: `public` and `none`.** The row said that what a customer role cannot take is what PostgreSQL itself reserves. That was not true of `postgres`, which is the node's superuser and not a PostgreSQL reservation, and it left out two names PostgreSQL does reserve. On PostgreSQL 18.6 in the pinned image `CREATE ROLE "public" LOGIN` and `CREATE ROLE "none" LOGIN` fail with `role name "public" is reserved` and `role name "none" is reserved`, quoted as well, and the agent always quotes (`quote_identifier` in `roles.rs`). `current_user`, `session_user`, `current_role` and `user` are accepted when quoted, so they stay ordinary names, and `pg_x` is refused by the prefix. Before this fix the contract, the API and the D1 `CHECK` took both names: `POST /roles` with `public` answered `201`. On the node `roles::apply` returns the `CREATE` error through `?`, so no later present role of that database is written either; on a running database `sync` only logs `roles_failed`, so the generation is never observed; at the next wake `refresh_roles` fails, the node stops the database unproven and answers `release_failed`, and recovery returns `Retry` on the same error and starts PostgreSQL again with backoff, without end. The database cannot wake again until the role is deleted. The two exact names are therefore reserved in this package with the other reserved names: `RESERVED_ROLE_NAMES`, the `CHECK` of `0085`, two node vectors (`NodeDesiredPage/role-public` and `role-none`) and the tests (decision `W2-C2` in 11.5; `current_user` and its siblings are kept as accepted names in the tests, so a later narrowing has to be deliberate). It is a narrowing with the same check and the same `0085` as `pgcf_backup`, and no further deploy step is needed (a later separate narrowing would need its own check and migration, then a release, then the Workers). A database that holds such a role today cannot wake, so a row found by the check is a database that needs the role deleted anyway. **Found in the fourth review, and fixed here (text only, no code changed): the order, the freeze and the cost of a refused page.** The row put R-2 before the migration and said that `wrangler d1 migrations apply` before R-2 "opens the names before the nodes accept them". That is not so: the old Workers still refuse the released names, so `0085` opens nothing, and it is what closes the three narrowed names, which the old API and D1 accepted from the first node on R-2 until the migration, while a node on R-2 refuses the page that names one. The order is now the check, `0085`, R-2, the API Worker and the Edge Worker; the migration freeze is dropped and the Worker freeze stays. The freeze as first written also held the dead capacity row's Worker and `0082` until R-2 had converged on every node and in every image; the row now says that Worker goes out before the merge or from the commit just before it. A refused page was described as a deadlock in which the node "can never receive a newer release". That overstated it, because a targeted pull for another database of the node is a valid page, carries the release and reaches `consider_update`, and it understated the cost: the agent's start retries the first full page without end and serves the gateway only after it, so a node below R-2 that holds such a role accepts no new connection for any of its databases from its next start on, and a rollback of a node below R-2 does the same. **Found in the fifth review, and fixed here (text only, no code changed): the deploy steps after the merge of `c54fca03`, and the cost of an API rollback.** Step (1) said that the apply runs `0082` and `0083` with `0085`, and the Freeze paragraph said that the Worker of `pr-w1c`, `pr-w1d` and `pr-w1e` is not deployed. Both went stale: the Done row "Release of main `69d2b245` live on EU1" records the API deployed with `0082_drop_dead_capacity_fields` and `0083_credentials_state`, so the apply runs `0085` alone. The precondition is now general: every API change on main at the moment this branch merges is deployed before the merge, or from the commit just before it, because R-2 is cut from main and carries that change's node side while the freeze would hold its API Worker back (example `pr-w2f`, if it merges first). The Rollback paragraph said that an API rollback "breaks the page or the role list of every database that holds such a role". That understated it: the old API cannot build the node page at all (`NodeDesiredPage.parse` with `RoleName`; `refineRoles` for `pgcf_maintenance`), so every full pull of the node and every targeted pull that names the database answers `500`, an agent start of that node never gets past the first full page, and the node accepts no new connection for any of its databases. The paragraph now says so, and that the API Worker is not rolled back below this change while such a role exists, unless those role rows are deleted in D1 first. **Found in the sixth review, and fixed here (text only, no code changed): a change that merges during the freeze.** The Freeze paragraph's precondition covered only the API changes on main at the moment this branch merges, and it said "No migration is frozen". The Merge note expected the other case, `pr-w2f` merging second (then numbered `0085`, with this migration as `0084`; the two have since swapped, see the Merge note): step (1) ran `wrangler d1 migrations apply` from main's head, which applies every pending migration, so the migration of `pr-w2f` would have run together with this one while the freeze forbade deploying `pr-w2f`'s Worker, and the deployed Worker, which reads the two dropped `regions` columns, would have failed in its archive credentials, moves and backup retention. Step (1) now applies this migration from the commit that merged this branch, after `wrangler d1 migrations list` shows it as the only pending migration, and the Freeze paragraph says that a change that merges during the freeze waits until step (3), Worker and migration alike (its migration after its Worker when it drops what the old Worker reads), or that no API change merges in between. The migration's header and the Open row say the same. **Found in the seventh review, and fixed here (text, the migration's header and `role-names-migration.test.ts`; no product code changed): the check missed the members, and the push of the merge.** (1) Step (0) and the Open row checked `roles.name` alone. The fix it prescribed, "a row found is deleted in D1 first", ignored the roles whose `member_of_json` names that row: the old API accepts `{"name":"x","member_of":["pgcf_backup"]}` while a `pgcf_backup` row is live, only the API's `DELETE` checks for members (`role_has_members`, `roles.ts`), and a hard delete in D1 does not. `x` then kept a membership of a role that is absent, `refineRoles` (`node-link.ts`) refused it, `NodeDesiredPage.parse` threw for the whole page, and the old API answered `500` to every full pull of the node, so that the agent that step (2) restarts never got past its first full page: the node-wide cost of (b), caused by the row's own fix. Even without a hard delete, `DesiredRole.member_of` is `RoleName[]` after step (3), which refuses the three names. The check now includes the members (`SELECT database_id, name FROM roles WHERE name IN ('pgcf_backup','public','none') OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(member_of_json) WHERE value IN ('pgcf_backup','public','none'))`), a row found is handled members first and rows second in one D1 batch, and a hit on `pgcf_backup` is said to leave barman's role on that database altered. The migration's header, the Open row and the decisions W2-C and W2-C2 in 11.5 give the same check. Red then green: in `role-names-migration.test.ts` the statements of the plan are run on a table that holds a `pgcf_backup` row, a role `x` that names it and a tombstone that names `public` (the check finds all three; after the row alone is deleted it still finds `x` and the tombstone, where a check on `roles.name` finds nothing; after the two statements it finds none, the lists keep every other name, and the migration runs), and a third test reads the statements from the plan and the migration's header character for character: it failed on the plan and the header (the check was not in either) and passes with them. (2) The Freeze paragraph said that R-2 is cut from the commit that merged this branch, and nothing said how the pipeline delivers that. It delivers it only when the merge commit is the head of its own push (`sign-release` runs on a push to main only, the release id is `sha-<first 12 digits of github.sha>`, GitHub runs CI for the head SHA of a push, and train 2 put four merges in one push), so the Freeze paragraph and step (2) now say that this merge is pushed alone, that its `sign-release` is green before anything else is pushed, that R-2 is the signed release `sha-<merge commit>`, and that its artifacts are kept for 7 days. **Found in the eighth review, and fixed here (text and the migration's header; no product code changed): the merge missed an API change, and the rollback missed the members.** (1) The merge of `f5d699c6` was made while `origin/main` already held `f09d26fb` and `c788749b` (the 3-day peak window of placement, owner decision O6, 11.3: `PEAK_WINDOW_MS` in `placement.ts` and a comment in `node-actor.ts`; API only, no migration, no node side; not deployed). Under the row's own precondition the Worker of `f09d26fb` is deployed before this branch merges, or from the commit just before it; otherwise the freeze holds the 3-day window back until step (3), and the md class and the restore into a smaller class, which 11.3 lets run once the 3-day release is deployed, wait for this row. Step (1), the Freeze paragraph and the Open row now name `f09d26fb` as pending, with its deploy as the precondition, and say what to record if it is deployed first. (2) Rollback and (b) said that the role rows are deleted in D1 and stopped there, which is the mistake of the seventh review in a second place: after a hard delete of `cnpg_app`, a role that names it in `member_of_json` keeps a membership of a role that is absent, and the old contract refuses that list anyway (`member_of` is `RoleName[]`, which refuses `cnpg_*` and `streaming_replica`), so the whole page still fails. The Rollback paragraph, (b) and the migration's header now say that the member lists lose the names first, in the order of step (0). Locally green after the merge of `origin/main` `c788749b`: contracts with the generator checks 27 files and 314 tests, API 109 files and 1,099 tests, Edge 119 tests, `scripts/ci` and `scripts/operations` 118 tests, typecheck, eslint, prettier and plan privacy; the merge brings no Rust change, so the Rust gates above are those of the last run after `f5d699c6`. **Live acceptance:** the Open row "Role names released: deploy and live acceptance (W2-C)" in 11.2.
| A database unit shares no IPC namespace, no journal and no writable place with another unit, and the agent starts none over a stray process, on branch `cold-sb` (package S, 2026-10-20, three rounds), not deployed | **Found.** The node lab (EU1, 2026-10-20) saw `/run/lock` (a 5 MiB tmpfs of the whole node, mode 1777) and `/dev/mqueue` (the host's queues, mode 1777) writable inside the full directive set of `pgcf-pg@.service`: a channel between tenants, files that outlive the unit, and a node-wide denial of service (LVM keeps its lock directory in `/run/lock`, and tmpfs inodes persist after the unit). It blocks the reuse of a user id. **Enumeration** (a Debian 13 container with systemd 257.13 as PID 1, privileged, arm64, the laptop's Docker VM; the repository's own unit with the volume bound from a directory; PostgreSQL 18.6; as the unit's user in the unit's mount and IPC namespaces; `find / -writable`). On main the set is: `/run/lock` and `/dev/mqueue` (directories, mode 1777); the host's SysV segments, because the unit is in PID 1's IPC namespace (a segment made by root there is listed in the unit, and PostgreSQL's own segment is in the host's namespace); and, found by the enumeration and not by the lab, `/dev/pts`: `PrivateDevices=yes` binds the host's devpts into the private `/dev` (the same `st_dev`), and the user opened 3071 `/dev/ptmx` before `ENOSPC` (3072 entries in the host's listing, about 11 MB of unreclaimable slab; it stopped at `kernel.pty.max` 4096 less `kernel.pty.reserve` 1024). The rest is the unit's own or holds no data (the volume, the socket directory, the private `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/dev/shm`, the pressure file of the unit's own cgroup; the character devices `null`, `zero`, `full`, `random`, `urandom`, `tty`; and the service sockets of the journal, systemd's notify and varlink sockets and D-Bus, each of which checks its caller); `infra/node-image/README.md` has each with its reason. **Change.** In the template: `PrivateIPC=yes`; `InaccessiblePaths=-/run/lock -/dev/mqueue -/dev/pts -/var/log/journal -/run/log/journal`; `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` as `TemporaryFileSystem=` of 16M and 1,024 files each, no longer `PrivateTmp=yes`. In the agent: `Units::start` refuses a start while its cgroup holds a process and the unit is not running or starting (`inactive`, `failed`, `deactivating`; `Error::StrayProcesses`). Measured on 257.13: `PrivateIPC=yes` alone gives a new IPC namespace and a mqueue instance of its own (`st_dev` 76 against 67; a file made in one is not in the other) but leaves it writable, which is the route around the seccomp denial of `mq_open` (a file created in the directory is the same queue), so the directory is inaccessible as well; the three paths then answer `EACCES` (`/var/lock` with `/run/lock`), no pty can be allocated, the listing of the host's `/dev/pts` has `ptmx` only, and the remaining writable directories and regular files are the unit's own. PostgreSQL 18.6 starts and serves in the unit (DDL and DML, a parallel query through dynamic shared memory in `/dev/shm`, a clean stop, a start after it); its SysV segment (56 bytes, 9 attached) is in the unit's namespace and the host's `ipcs` does not list it; `systemd-analyze security` still rates it SAFE (0.4 with round 1, 0.5 with round 2). The same unit with its own `MountImages=` line (the volume an ext4 image file with systemd's loop device, from the link `/run/pgcf/dev/<id>`) started and passed the same checks and the same smoke test. **The interlock (corrected in round 2).** README and Appendix C said `PrivateIPC` must stay off because of `postmaster.pid`; the sources of PostgreSQL 18 (`miscinit.c`: `kill()` answering `EPERM` is read as a stale file; `sysv_shmem.c`: `EINVAL` is no segment and `EACCES` a foreign one, both "not in use") and the lab show which half it takes. PostgreSQL refuses a second postmaster in two ways: the pid in `postmaster.pid` is alive (`kill(pid, 0)`, which needs the shared PID namespace, so `PrivatePIDs` stays off), and the SysV segment named there is still attached. The pid half refuses a second postmaster of the same user at once ("lock file postmaster.pid already exists", exit 1, the first one unharmed, with the second in an IPC namespace of its own). The segment half is what guards against a backend that outlives its postmaster, and a new IPC namespace at every start blinds it. Lab (systemd 257.13, PostgreSQL 18.6; found by the independent verification of round 1 and reproduced in this change's container): a backend stopped (`SIGSTOP`), its postmaster killed (`SIGKILL`), and the segment stayed attached (`nattch` 1); a second postmaster in the same IPC namespace was refused ("pre-existing shared memory block ... is still in use"); one in a new IPC namespace, which is what `PrivateIPC=yes` gives every start, ran "database system was not properly shut down; automatic recovery in progress" while the old backend was alive. The real path is a backend in uninterruptible sleep through both stop timeouts ("Processes still around after final SIGKILL"): the unit is `failed` with a process in its cgroup, the sleep proof fails, the agent recovers the database by starting the unit, and systemd starts a unit over a process of its cgroup ("Found left-over process ... while starting unit. Ignoring."). Before S the segment check refused that start. **Fix (round 2, corrected in round 3).** `Units::start` reads the unit's `cgroup.events` and refuses a start while the cgroup says `populated 1` and the unit is not `active`, `reloading`, `activating` or `refreshing`, so `inactive`, `failed` and `deactivating` are refused (`Error::StrayProcesses`, diagnostic class `units_stray_processes`; round 2 let `deactivating` through, see **The deactivating window** below); a stopped unit has no cgroup, so the common path is one failed `open`, and a unit that runs, starts or reloads is passed on to systemd as before. The wake or the recovery fails like any failed start, is tried again, and goes through when the process is gone. Red then green in the lab (round 2, this change's container, the repository's unit with its own `MountImages=`): a test stopped a backend, killed the postmaster with `SendSIGKILL=no` so that the process stays (the stand-in for uninterruptible sleep), restored the template's kill setting, and asked for a start in `failed`: without the check the start succeeded and a new postmaster ran beside the stopped backend; with it the start was refused, the unit stayed `failed` with its old invocation, and after the backend was killed the next start went through and a start of the running unit joined it. Round 3 replaced that test with one that covers `deactivating` as well and uses a process that really no signal ends (**The deactivating window**, below). Without systemd, `stray_processes` is tested for every unit state and `cgroup.events` text. Of another user neither half of the interlock refuses (`EPERM` reads as stale, an unreadable segment as foreign): a database has one user, so the agent's one writer per database and this refusal are the guards, and a pooled slot user (11.2) needs the lock of the agent's supervisor first. All 16 tests of `units::lab` pass with the change.

That rule made the users ahead only up to the highest slot in use plus twice `start_concurrency`, so a storm larger than that failed its excess wakes with `units_no_slot` until the node was quiet again; "the acceptance storm reports it" was wrong, because the acceptance storm (20 wakes) never reaches the 24 numbers of EU1, and the rule is replaced in round 3 (finding 1, below). (f) *The binding rule is atomic:* `bind` looked at `release_ended` before `take`, and `take` never looked again, so two binds of one database that passed the first check together claimed two slots, and a slot being built held no database. The claim is one step under the table's lock in which no slot may hold the database, and a slot being built is entered for its database from `reserve`. Before P-e and in round 1 those wakes succeeded, slower. On EU1 (`start_concurrency` 8) it was every wake past the 24th of a storm until the node was quiet again, and the admission queue is bounded only by `queue_wait_ms`. **Red:** `a_storm_larger_than_the_idle_slots_and_twice_the_target_finds_a_number_for_every_wake` (a node that never made a slot, the refill until 8 idle slots, 30 binds of distinct databases) failed on the code of round 2 with `wakes that failed: [(24, "every slot is in use"), (25, ...), ... (29, ...)]`. **Fix, with the judge's item 11 kept (no user on the wake path):** `Pool::make_users` is replaced by `Pool::make_user` (the lowest number without a user, one per call, a number whose user failed skipped), and `Core::refill_pass` calls it through `Machine::make_slot_user` once the idle slots are in place and while `Admission::quiet()`, until every number of the pool's range 0 to 1022 has its user: the users are made in the quiet passes ahead of any need and persist in `/etc/passwd`. `Pool::refill` makes only the one user an idle slot needs where no free number has one (a node that never made a slot, and the health check's slot 1023). The cost is 1023 users at 74 ms (container), about 75 s of the first quiet passes of a node's life, once; a node just installed has only the users made so far until then, and a wake that finds none free fails as before. Using up all 1023 numbers would take more than a thousand awake databases of at least 256 MiB. Tests: the storm test above (green), `a_miss_never_makes_a_user_and_the_refill_makes_them_ahead` and `a_number_whose_user_cannot_be_made_is_skipped` (rewritten for `make_user`), and `the_refill_makes_the_users_of_the_whole_range_while_the_node_is_quiet` (a start in flight makes no user; the quiet pass makes all 1023), which failed with the user step removed from `refill_pass` (4 users of 1023) and with its quiet check removed (1023 users while a start is in flight, 4 expected). A node that had only the users of the slots it built (a fresh node, the first quiet passes after this release reaches EU1, or any time load keeps the node from being quiet) took the failed number again and again for as long as the stray process lived, and its wakes failed with it. The verification showed it three ways: the lab test `the_kernel_lets_one_slot_run_a_postmaster_on_a_data_directory_and_postgresql_alone_would_let_two` failed 10 of 10 at `assert_ne!(restarted.slot, first.slot)` (900 and 900), a scratch unit test (users {0}, number 0 stuck: three `refill(1)` all `Err`, users stay {0}), and round 3's gates had not re-run the lab while its row said all eight pass. **Fix.** `Table::fresh_number` is the lowest number that is free, has a user and did not fail last; `free_number` is a fresh one or, where every free number with a user failed, the lowest of those. `Pool::refill` makes the next user when there is no fresh number and then builds on a fresh number, or on a failed one as the last resort; a user that cannot be made does not end it (its error is the one returned only where no number is left). `Core::refill_pass` no longer returns on a failed build: it goes on to `make_slot_user`, which ends the pass when it has nothing left to make, so the loop is bounded by the range. **Red then green.** Each of these failed on a copy of the tree with the fix undone and passes with it: `a_refill_makes_a_user_when_every_free_number_with_one_has_failed` (a fresh node, users {0}, number 0 stuck: the second `refill` returned `Err(StrayProcesses)` and made no user; now it makes user 1, builds there and the next wake takes that idle slot), `a_refill_that_cannot_make_the_next_user_still_tries_the_failed_number` (user 1 cannot be made; the third refill returned `Err(StrayProcesses)` before and builds on number 2 now) and `a_failed_build_does_not_end_the_refill_before_it_makes_the_next_user` (`agent/power.rs`, the `Local` test machine with the user of number 0 only and a unit that refuses its start, as the real one does over a stray process: before, 0 idle slots and one user; now one idle slot on the next number and the users of the whole range); `a_refill_where_no_user_can_be_made_names_the_user` guards the error. The lab test now makes the users of the range with `Pool::make_user` before the kill, as the quiet passes of a node that has run for a while have: a wake makes none (judge's item 11), so a number that failed is kept out only while another number with a user is free, and the lab stands for that node. **The journal (round 2).** Verified on EU1 (371 files) and in the lab: journald's `SplitMode=uid` writes `user-<uid>.journal` with a POSIX ACL that grants that uid read access, `release()` frees a uid when its database leaves the node, `remove_account` deletes no journal file, and a later database with that uid reads the former owner's log (lab: a process with the uid of a deleted database read its file, another uid did not; eight such files after the lab's deleted databases). This is a leak without the pool, and the previous text ("no leak while a user id belongs to one database for good") was wrong; section 8, `README.md` and the header of `units/users.rs` are corrected. The unit's `InaccessiblePaths=-/var/log/journal -/run/log/journal` closes it for the database's user; logging through `/run/systemd/journal/stdout` is unaffected (PostgreSQL's lines are in the journal by invocation, which is how the agent reads them). `SplitMode=none` as a host file stays with the pool (package P).

**Scratch space and the socket directory (round 2).** The private `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` of `PrivateTmp=yes` were directories on the host's root filesystem (8 GiB on EU1, no quota; disk blocks are no memory that `MemoryMax` counts): an awake tenant could fill it, which stops the journal and the agent's state writes for the whole node. They are tmpfs of 16M and 1,024 files each now (`noexec,nosuid,nodev`, as the 64 MiB of `/dev/shm`); their pages are the unit's memory; PostgreSQL uses neither; it served a parallel query through `/dev/shm` as before. The socket directory `/run/pgcf/<id>` is the other place the plan called "the unit's own" that shares node capacity, and it stays open: lab, `MemoryMax` 256 MiB, `MemoryHigh` 230 MiB, no swap: a tenant's file there is charged to the unit while it runs (the writer is throttled at `MemoryHigh` and stops near 245 MiB) and stays after the unit stops (215 MiB used in `/run` after the stop, charged to `pgcf.slice`); the remedy is the Open row in 11.2. The statement "nothing a database's user writes outlives its unit outside its own volume" was false for it and is corrected in section 8.

**Sockets and FIFOs (round 2).** The list of endpoints a database's user can reach had left out the agent's archive socket: `/run/pgcf/agent/archive.sock` (mode 0666 in `RuntimeDirectory=pgcf/agent`, mode 0755; `archive/server.rs`), which every database's archive command calls and which authorizes by `SO_PEERCRED` uid alone (it matters for a uid used twice, section 8). `README.md` lists it with the journal's, notify, varlink and D-Bus sockets, each with its reason, and the boot test's enumeration is extended from `-type d -o -type f` to sockets and FIFOs against an explicit list (the lab container, an image of the same systemd: the writable sockets are the journal's three, `/run/systemd/notify`, `io.systemd.Hostname`, `Credentials`, `ManagedOOM` and `userdb/io.systemd.DynamicUser`, and D-Bus's; `/run/initctl` and `/run/systemd/private` are root's). Negative control in the lab: a stray socket and a FIFO made in `/run/pgcf` fail the new check, and the round 1 check passes with them.

**The deactivating window (round 3).** The independent verification of round 2 found that the refusal let a start through while the unit was `deactivating`: the refusal used `awake()`, which counts `deactivating`, and the unit test pinned `(Deactivating, true)` as no stray. **The failing state** (systemd 257.13, Debian 13 container): the postmaster dies on its own, a backend in uninterruptible sleep survives the kill signals, and the unit is `deactivating` with `MainPID` 0 and `populated 1`, in `stop-sigkill` and then `final-sigkill` (each `TimeoutStopSec`, so up to 60 s with the template's 30 s; there is no `stop-sigterm` stage, because `KillMode=mixed` signals the main process only and it is gone), and no job. Job mode `fail` refuses a start only against a pending job (measured: a start asked for while a stop job is pending answers "Transaction for ... is destructive"), so systemd accepted the start as a job that waits, and ran it when the unit ended in `failed` ("Processes still around after final SIGKILL"), over the process, with the new postmaster in a new IPC namespace beside it. The agent reaches the window by its own path: it (re)starts, adopts the unit it finds (`AdoptRunning`; `wait_started` answers `unit_not_active` for `deactivating`), goes unproven, and the recovery starts the unit. **Fix.** `stray_processes` refuses when the cgroup is populated and the unit is anything but `active`, `reloading`, `activating` or `refreshing`, `deactivating` included; `awake()` is unchanged, because the memory accounting still counts a stopping unit. No legitimate start changes: a start asked for while a stop job is pending failed in job mode `fail` before and now fails with `StrayProcesses`, and the recovery retries with its back-off as before. **Tests.** Red then green. The unit test (renamed `a_process_is_a_stray_unless_the_unit_runs_or_starts_it`) has the `Deactivating` row flipped from awake to a stray: red with `left: false, right: true` for `Deactivating`, green with the change. The lab test `a_start_is_refused_while_the_unit_stops_over_a_process_no_signal_ends` (`units/lab.rs`; it replaces round 2's `SendSIGKILL=no` test and covers what that did): the database's filesystem is frozen with `fsfreeze`, a `CHECKPOINT` makes a process of the unit write to it and sleep in the kernel (`D`), the postmaster gets `SIGKILL`, and the unit is observed `deactivating` with no main process and a populated cgroup; the start asked for then must be refused (red: it is accepted and waits behind the stop, `Err(Elapsed)` after 2 s), the unit then ends `failed` with the process still in its cgroup and a start is refused again with the old invocation unchanged, and after the thaw the cgroup empties, the start goes through and a start of the running unit joins it. Sampled in the lab with `TimeoutStopSec=3`: `active` at 1.45 s, `deactivating`/`stop-sigkill` at 1.69 s, `final-sigkill` at 4.72 s, the end about 3 s later. Ten runs green, all 16 tests of `units::lab` pass. **Not covered.** EU1 (the live acceptance, item 4 of the Open row, now covers `deactivating`).

**Cost.** Fork to handoff (`ExecMainHandoff` minus `ExecMainStart`) of the unit of main (`a23d7f11`), of round 1 and of round 2, interleaved, volume mounted with `MountImages=` from a loop device image, arm64 Docker VM (kernel 6.8): p50 73.0, 78.9 and 75.9 ms in 40 triples, 56.8, 61.9 and 59.9 ms in 60 triples, so round 2 is +3.0 and +3.1 ms over main at p50 (the p95 of 40 and 60 samples is not claimed). Round 1 measured about 0.5 ms with the volume bound from a directory. EU1 is open (11.2). **Tests.** Red on the previous state, green with the change. `units.test.ts`: the template carries `PrivateIPC=yes`, the five inaccessible paths and no other, tmpfs of 16M with 1,024 files for `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` with `noexec,nosuid,nodev`, and neither `PrivateTmp` nor `PrivatePIDs`. `guest.sh` against round 1's template in the lab container: `database_user_reads_no_journal` fails with three findings (the user reads its own `user-<uid>.journal`; both directories answer a listing), `database_scratch_space_is_bounded` fails with six (`/tmp` and `/var/tmp` are not tmpfs within 16 MiB and 1,024 files, and a write of 17 MiB succeeds in both); with the change both pass, as do `database_user_shares_nothing_writable` (extended to sockets and FIFOs), `database_second_postmaster_is_refused` and PostgreSQL's smoke test. Round 1's red results: `database_user_shares_nothing_writable` against the template of main fails with ten findings (a file created in `/run/lock` and in `/dev/mqueue`, neither refused, `/dev/pts` listed and a pty allocated, the unit in PID 1's IPC namespace, the host's SysV segment visible, PostgreSQL's segment in the host's namespace, `/run/lock` and `/dev/mqueue` among the writable directories). The host file stays `next_start`, so a running unit takes the change at its next start. **Not covered.** The KVM boot test (CI runs it on the image; the new checks ran only in the lab container, and the enumeration of directories, files, sockets and FIFOs may name a path of the image that the lab lacks, which is added to the test only if it is the unit's own or an endpoint that checks its caller); EU1; the backup jobs (`archive/job.rs`), which run as the database's user with a smaller set and still see the host's `/run/lock` and `/dev/mqueue`, because they run the node's barman and not a tenant's code. |
